CLAT 2027 MOCK TEST – 28

                                           Instructions:

      •   Time allowed: 2 hours.
      •   Total Questions: 120.
      •   Once done with the mock test, mark the answers on the portal to get your score.
      •   Try to complete the entire mock, do not get disheartened while doing it.
      •   Try to concentrate properly for 2 hours, we are with you.
      •   Do not forget to analyse after you are done.


                                     DATA INTEPRETATION
A municipal corporation awards a road-widening contract to a construction firm. The firm deploys three
specialised teams: Team Alpha, Team Beta, and Team Gamma to execute the project. Working
independently and at constant rates, Alpha can complete the project in 10 days, Beta in 15 days, and
Gamma in 6 days.
To optimise resource utilisation, the project manager adopts a phased deployment plan. In Phase I, all
three teams work together for exactly one day. Under the deployment schedule, Alpha is required to
remain on the project for exactly 3 days before being reassigned elsewhere. Accordingly, in Phase II,
Alpha and Beta continue working together for two additional days, after which Alpha exits the project.
In Phase III, Beta completes the remaining work alone.
The operational costs remain fixed throughout the project. Alpha costs ₹12,000 per day, Beta ₹9,000
per day, and Gamma ₹6,000 per day. The corporation has allocated a budget of ₹1,20,000 for the
project, and any expenditure below this amount is treated as a cost saving for the firm. As part of its
project review, the firm also evaluates an alternative deployment strategy. Under this plan, Gamma
works alone for the first two days before standing down, following which Alpha and Beta jointly
complete the remaining work. The firm compares both deployment strategies to assess their impact on
project cost and completion time.
content.questionText:
In the original phased arrangement described in the passage, what is the total number of days taken
to complete the project?
options: 6 days
7 days
8 days
9 days

content.passageText:
Meridian Corp employs 360 people across three departments: Sales, Marketing, and Operations, in the
ratio 3:4:5, respectively. The average monthly salary in Sales is ₹60,000 per employee, and in

Operations, it is ₹36,000 per employee. The average monthly salary across the entire organisation,
including all three departments, is ₹46,000 per employee.

Each department also has a fixed internal gender split: in Sales, the ratio of male to female employees
is 2:1, in Marketing, it is 3:5, and in Operations, employees are split equally between the two genders.
Independently, the company’s HR audit reports that the average monthly salary of all male employees,
across departments, is ₹50,000, while the average monthly salary of all female employees, across
departments, is ₹42,000. Within any given department, all employees, regardless of gender, are paid
the department’s average salary unless otherwise stated.

As part of a board-approved restructuring, departmental pay scales will be revised with effect from the
next financial year: Sales salaries will remain unchanged, Marketing salaries will be cut by 20% (owing
to a fall in incentive-linked pay), and Operations salaries will rise by 25% (to align with industry
benchmarks). Separately, after this departmental revision takes effect, the company will also grant a
one-time flat top-up to every employee, irrespective of department: ₹2,000 per month to every male
employee and ₹1,500 per month to every female employee, in recognition of the year’s performance.
All workforce numbers, departmental figures, and gender-wise figures given above are mutually
consistent, and no employee belongs to more than one department or gender category.
content.questionText:
Before any revision, what is the ratio of the total monthly salary bill of all male employees to the
total monthly salary bill of all female employees, across the entire organisation?

content.passageText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS
In the scheme of the Indian Constitution, the fundamental rights enumerated in Part III, form a
fundamental limitation on the powers of the state. This is evidenced by Article 13(2), which provides
that any law made, which abridges or abolishes any of the rights in Part III, will to the extent of
contravention, be void' . During an emergency situation, where the security of the nation is at stake, it
is, however, essential that the state is equipped with adequate powers to deal with the situation in the
best possible manner. It therefore becomes necessary to remove the restriction imposed on State power
by Part III to a limited extent. At the same time, the restrictions cannot be removed so as to completely
obliterate individuals' rights. Part XVIII of the Constitution, which contains the emergency provisions,
seeks to provide a balance between the two ends; giving the State increased powers to deal with the
situation and at the same time ensuring that some of the basic rights in Part III remain intact. Over the
last 50 years, an emergency on account of the security of the nation being threatened has been
proclaimed on three occasions. In 1962, during the Chinese invasion, in 1971 during the conflict with
Pakistan and once again in 1975 on account of internal disturbance . On all three occasions, the judiciary
has had occasion to examine the impact of the proclamation on fundamental rights.
content.questionText:
Which constitutional amendment altered the operational mechanics of Article 352 by enabling the
President to restrict the application of a National Emergency to a specified geographical region rather
than the entire country?
options: 38th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975
39th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

In the scheme of the Indian Constitution, the fundamental rights enumerated in Part III, form a
fundamental limitation on the powers of the state. This is evidenced by Article 13(2), which provides
that any law made, which abridges or abolishes any of the rights in Part III, will to the extent of
contravention, be void' . During an emergency situation, where the security of the nation is at stake, it
is, however, essential that the state is equipped with adequate powers to deal with the situation in the
best possible manner. It therefore becomes necessary to remove the restriction imposed on State power
by Part III to a limited extent. At the same time, the restrictions cannot be removed so as to completely
obliterate individuals' rights. Part XVIII of the Constitution, which contains the emergency provisions,
seeks to provide a balance between the two ends; giving the State increased powers to deal with the
situation and at the same time ensuring that some of the basic rights in Part III remain intact. Over the
last 50 years, an emergency on account of the security of the nation being threatened has been
proclaimed on three occasions. In 1962, during the Chinese invasion, in 1971 during the conflict with
Pakistan and once again in 1975 on account of internal disturbance . On all three occasions, the judiciary
has had occasion to examine the impact of the proclamation on fundamental rights.

content.passageText:
The demand to transition away from fossil fuels is no longer only a whisper that many don’t have the
courage to say out loud; it’s a universal cry for survival: we need to equitably move away from the
extraction plotting our destruction. We need a global transition away from fossil fuels that is fast, fair,
and financed — one that strengthens energy sovereignty, stabilises economies, and supports workers
and communities, leaving no one behind. All countries now face a stark choice: either unite to forge
equitable new forms of international cooperation to deliver a fast and funded transition away from fossil
fuels, or remain dangerously vulnerable to volatile supply shocks and the global conflicts they fuel. The
Santa Marta Conference is the decisive opportunity to strengthen international cooperation by finally
confronting these interconnected crises at their shared source. It is a historic turning point in climate
diplomacy, and a fundamental act for global stability. Tired of waiting for an elusive consensus,
committed, high-ambition nations are coming together, ready to move from incremental pledges to
concrete action. They will champion coordinated solutions, including strengthening multilateralism to
address the threat of fossil fuel extraction. This is why a global coalition of nation-states, subnational
governments, Indigenous peoples, scientists and civil society will arrive in Santa Marta calling for
countries to participate in the development of a Fossil Fuel Treaty as a key outcome of the summit.

On 23 April, 2025, India put the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) of 1960 with Pakistan in abeyance, by
temporarily suspending it under certain conditions. The move followed the Pahalgam attack in India,
carried out by a supposedly Pakistan-based militant group, and was made during the subsequent military
escalation. The Indian government cited national security concerns and Pakistan’s alleged support of
state-sponsored terrorism as reasons for this step. The temporary suspension of one of the world’s most
conflict resilient water-sharing agreements is an extraordinary development and marks a surprising,
serious and harsh act. For over six decades, the IWT endured various diplomatic breakdowns, violent
escalations, and full-scale wars between India and Pakistan as well as surging nationalism on both sides,
without being seriously questioned by either party. That it now falters signals a shift not only in the
India-Pakistan relations but also in the geopolitics of the region and the politics and management of
shared water resources. This Alert examines the implications of the temporary suspension of the IWT,
not only as a strategic move in the India-Pakistan crisis and a geopolitical rupture but also as a pivotal
moment from a water perspective. It reaffirms cooperation necessities while allowing for renewed
thinking about and around transboundary water governance.

The potential of this partnership shall enable disseminating bench marked practices from big cat range
countries which have successfully implemented wildlife conservation initiatives, result in target
oriented capacity building initiatives which shall lead to tangible outputs and outcomes and at the same
time make available a common pool of resources which can be harnessed by any big cat range country
based on felt requirements and needs. The partnership also aims to strengthen the existing species-
specific inter-governmental platforms, networks and transnational initiatives on conservation and
protection. A partnership is envisaged, to consist of countries, majority of whom face similar challenges
resulting in depressed big cat numbers besides poor status of prey and degraded habitats, which would
be based on the long standing tiger and other big cat good practices evolved in India, primarily and
elsewhere in the range countries. Big Cat Range Countries can share their experiences and mobilize
resources in order to close prevalent gaps by cooperating with each other, solutions will be found and

will also be scaled up leading to lower implementation costs. The IBCA's multi-pronged approach will
enhance linkages, promote knowledge sharing, capacity building, networking, advocacy, finance,
research, technical support, insurance against failures, education, awareness, employment, and
sustainable local livelihoods. Establishment of IBCA will, thus, neither duplicate nor undermine the
efforts what other cross-national bodies are already doing, but will establish and develop synergies and

ENGLISH LANGUAGE

On November 12, Delhi’s air unbreathable. A thick blanket of smog enveloped the capital, which
recorded an average Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 400, and the pollution was categorised as “severe.”
On November 9, Delhiites, aware of the possible respiratory ailments this relapsing crisis could lead to,
protested at India Gate. Many were detained. Meanwhile, in April, the India Meteorological Department
(IMD) and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, released a three-decade study showing
that rainwater in several parts of the country was becoming increasingly “acidic.”


But can we authoritatively attribute these environmental catastrophes to human-induced climate
change? Put another way, while the irrefutable fact is the earth has warmed by more than 1o C since
pre-industrial times, thanks to human-generated greenhouse gases and there are local events that result
in local environmental disasters as well, how sure we can we be that climate change made a cloudburst
or a cyclone more likely? This is where climate attribution science comes in. This field is concerned
with estimating how the probability of events or their intensity, duration or frequency are altered by
climate change.


“Models try to create a world where climate change didn’t happen and look at the real world where
events happened,” Earth System Scientist Raghu Murtugudde explained. “Models are imperfect, and
depending on which of these changes you try to estimate, you can get different answers. An event may
have occurred naturally but attribution may say its intensity was made stronger or that its probability
was increased, and so on,” he told The Hindu. In general the attribution of heat waves is more accurate
than the attribution of extreme rain events, J. Srinivasan, honorary professor at the Divecha Centre for
Climate Change, said. “When a major heat wave strikes Europe or Asia, scientists try to estimate the
contribution of the increase in carbon dioxide to that particular heat wave. Their attribution will be
accurate if the model is good at simulating the past heat waves in that region,” Prof. Srinivasan said.
SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/energy-and-environment/can-climate-attribution-
science-save-lives/article70274326.ece

content.passageText:
Long, long ago there lived at the foot of the mountain a poor farmer and his aged, widowed mother.
They owned a bit of land which supplied them with food, and they were humble, peaceful, and happy.
Shining was governed by a despotic leader who though a warrior, had a great and cowardly shrinking
from anything suggestive of failing health and strength. This led him to issue a cruel proclamation. The
entire province was given strict orders to immediately put to death all aged people. Those were
barbarous days, and the custom of abandoning old people to die was not uncommon.


The poor farmer loved his aged mother with tender reverence, and the order filled his heart with sorrow.
But no one ever thought twice about obeying the mandate of the governor, so with many deep and
hopeless sighs, the youth prepared for what at that time was considered the kindest mode of death. Just
at sundown, when his day’s work was ended, he took a quantity of unwhitened rice which was the
principal food for the poor, and he cooked, dried it, and tied it in a square cloth, which he swung in a
bundle around his neck along with a gourd filled with cool, sweet water. Then he lifted his helpless old
mother to his back and started on his painful journey up the mountain. On he went, climbing blindly
upward -- ever upward towards the high bare summit of what is known as Obatsuyama, the mountain
of the “abandoning of the aged.”


The eyes of the old mother were not so dim but that they noted the reckless hastening from one path to
another, and her loving heart grew anxious. Her son did not know the mountain’s many paths and his
return might be one of danger, so she stretched forth her hand and snapping the twigs from brushes as
they passed, she quietly dropped a handful every few steps of the way so that as they climbed, the
narrow path behind them was dotted at frequent intervals with tiny piles of twigs. At last the summit
was reached. Weary and heart sick, the youth gently released his burden and silently prepared a place
of comfort as his last duty to the loved one. Gathering fallen pine needles, he made a soft cushion and
tenderly lifted his old mother onto it. He wrapped her padded coat more closely about the stooping
shoulders and with tearful eyes and an aching heart he said farewell.
SOURCE: https://americanliterature.com/author/matsuo-basho/short-story/the-aged-mother

content.passageText:
Long, long ago there lived at the foot of the mountain a poor farmer and his aged, widowed mother.
They owned a bit of land which supplied them with food, and they were humble, peaceful, and happy.
Shining was governed by a despotic leader who though a warrior, had a great and cowardly shrinking
from anything suggestive of failing health and strength. This led him to issue a cruel proclamation. The
entire province was given strict orders to immediately put to death all aged people. Those were
barbarous days, and the custom of abandoning old people to die was not uncommon.


The poor farmer loved his aged mother with tender reverence, and the order filled his heart with sorrow.
But no one ever thought twice about obeying the mandate of the governor, so with many deep and
hopeless sighs, the youth prepared for what at that time was considered the kindest mode of death. Just
at sundown, when his day’s work was ended, he took a quantity of unwhitened rice which was the
principal food for the poor, and he cooked, dried it, and tied it in a square cloth, which he swung in a
bundle around his neck along with a gourd filled with cool, sweet water. Then he lifted his helpless old
mother to his back and started on his painful journey up the mountain. On he went, climbing blindly
upward -- ever upward towards the high bare summit of what is known as Obatsuyama, the mountain
of the “abandoning of the aged.”


The eyes of the old mother were not so dim but that they noted the reckless hastening from one path to
another, and her loving heart grew anxious. Her son did not know the mountain’s many paths and his
return might be one of danger, so she stretched forth her hand and snapping the twigs from brushes as
they passed, she quietly dropped a handful every few steps of the way so that as they climbed, the
narrow path behind them was dotted at frequent intervals with tiny piles of twigs. At last the summit
was reached. Weary and heart sick, the youth gently released his burden and silently prepared a place
of comfort as his last duty to the loved one. Gathering fallen pine needles, he made a soft cushion and
tenderly lifted his old mother onto it. He wrapped her padded coat more closely about the stooping
shoulders and with tearful eyes and an aching heart he said farewell.

content.passageText:
The Supreme Court’s recall of its May 2025 Vanashakti judgment, which barred ex post facto
environmental clearances (EC) — a mechanism to regularise violations “in exceptional circumstances”
— weakens environmental regulation in the country. The majority decision to recall the judgment not
only buttresses the acceptability of regularising environmental non-compliance but also undermines the

deterrence value of the regulatory regime. The majority decision leans heavily on the costs of
dismantling projects that violated the environmental clearance regime; it cites financial costs —
especially public finances for some projects — and environmental costs, including increased pollution
following demolition. It also says that the State can’t be totally denuded of its power to grant
relaxations.


However, it is difficult to see how these considerations outweigh the costs of ex post facto EC. The
mechanism, instituted through an environment ministry notification in 2017 as a one-time reprieve,
effectively diluted the precautionary principle in environmental regulation that ensured a regime
oriented towards prevention of harm rather than compensation and atonement under the “polluter pays”
principle. Regularising past breaches meant legitimising non-compliance and diminishing
environmental safeguards that deterred projects ill-suited to the ecology of their proposed sites. Given
that it drew on environment ministry office memorandums (OMs) from 2012 and 2013, both of which
had been struck down by the courts, it also ran contrary to the established jurisprudence on the need for
prior environmental approval.


Reviving the ex post facto EC regime reinforces regularisation of non-compliance, bartered for a
financial penalty. Despite government assurances in 2017 that this was a one-time mechanism — with
the window for seeking clearances ending six months after notification — and that future clearances
would require public hearings, a 2021 OM reversed that stance. This, along with the top court’s recall,
creates a moral hazard in which project proponents don’t see the prior approval regime as a deterrent.
Breaches get incentivised, especially when penalties do not pinch or where business gains outweigh the
fines. India’s environmental regulation draws from many sources, including judicial interpretations of
laws, regulatory provisions, and constitutional mandates. But on a first-principles basis, it needs to
prioritise environmental interests over other concerns. The Court’s recall falls significantly short on this
count.
.

clearances-diluting-green-protection-101763566263714.html

content.passageText:
Whenever a film like Dhurandhar releases, the reaction follows a wearyingly predictable pattern. On
one side, a segment of critics dismisses it as state-sponsored propaganda; on the other, enthusiasts
embrace it as a long-overdue call to patriotism. Yet, to step into a crowded theatre in Delhi, Mumbai,
or Lucknow is to witness a phenomenon that bypasses these ideological skirmishes. What we see is not

an audience succumbing to a “message,” but a public experiencing the profound catharsis of
recognition. For the person in the seat, this is not about politics; it is about a story that finally feels like
their own. What truly unsettles the critics is not the film’s creative liberty, but its disconcerting
proximity to the truth.


For decades, India’s response to crisis was one of restraint and hesitation. Dhurandhar encapsulates a
“new template of response,” one that is resilient, proactive, and self-assured. Those who take issue with
this movie are, in fact, highlighting their own discomfort with an India that is no longer content to be a
perpetual victim. When we look at the global reception of such films, a glaring double standard emerges.
The world has long applauded the “Top Gun” bravado of American cinema. From Zero Dark Thirty
and Black Hawk Down to American Sniper and Lone Survivor, Hollywood has a long-standing tradition
of releasing high-octane films following major military operations or wars to stir national pride and
process collective trauma. These films are celebrated globally as expressions of cultural confidence and
“soft power.” Why, then, is Indian cinema subjected to a different yardstick?


Our soft power is no longer just about the passive beauty of our heritage; it is becoming a deliberate,
muscular articulation of our national journey. Just as Western cinema creates narratives to validate its
national interests, India is now using film to define its own stance on the global stage. One of the film’s
most powerful elements is its portrayal of the actual face of Indian security, a face that is inherently
pluralistic. Their interactions serve as a reminder that the ramparts of Indian security are not manned
by a single identity, but by a kaleidoscopic mosaic of faiths and backgrounds. The debates surrounding
the film are essential because they signal that India is no longer indifferent to how its story is told. For
the person sitting in the darkened theatre, this is a moment of profound recognition. They are seeing the
challenges they felt and the heroes they knew existed but rarely saw honoured on screen. At long last,
the story finally belongs to them.


SOURCE: https://www.thestatesman.com/opinion/catharsis-of-recognition-1503574264.html

content.passageText:
Whenever a film like Dhurandhar releases, the reaction follows a wearyingly predictable pattern. On
one side, a segment of critics dismisses it as state-sponsored propaganda; on the other, enthusiasts
embrace it as a long-overdue call to patriotism. Yet, to step into a crowded theatre in Delhi, Mumbai,
or Lucknow is to witness a phenomenon that bypasses these ideological skirmishes. What we see is not

an audience succumbing to a “message,” but a public experiencing the profound catharsis of
recognition. For the person in the seat, this is not about politics; it is about a story that finally feels like
their own. What truly unsettles the critics is not the film’s creative liberty, but its disconcerting
proximity to the truth.


For decades, India’s response to crisis was one of restraint and hesitation. Dhurandhar encapsulates a
“new template of response,” one that is resilient, proactive, and self-assured. Those who take issue with
this movie are, in fact, highlighting their own discomfort with an India that is no longer content to be a
perpetual victim. When we look at the global reception of such films, a glaring double standard emerges.
The world has long applauded the “Top Gun” bravado of American cinema. From Zero Dark Thirty
and Black Hawk Down to American Sniper and Lone Survivor, Hollywood has a long-standing tradition
of releasing high-octane films following major military operations or wars to stir national pride and
process collective trauma. These films are celebrated globally as expressions of cultural confidence and
“soft power.” Why, then, is Indian cinema subjected to a different yardstick?


Our soft power is no longer just about the passive beauty of our heritage; it is becoming a deliberate,
muscular articulation of our national journey. Just as Western cinema creates narratives to validate its
national interests, India is now using film to define its own stance on the global stage. One of the film’s
most powerful elements is its portrayal of the actual face of Indian security, a face that is inherently
pluralistic. Their interactions serve as a reminder that the ramparts of Indian security are not manned
by a single identity, but by a kaleidoscopic mosaic of faiths and backgrounds. The debates surrounding
the film are essential because they signal that India is no longer indifferent to how its story is told. For
the person sitting in the darkened theatre, this is a moment of profound recognition. They are seeing the
challenges they felt and the heroes they knew existed but rarely saw honoured on screen. At long last,
the story finally belongs to them.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman’s visit to the White House marked the official end of a
brief chill in relations between the most powerful country and the most influential Arab state. Ties had
hit a low after Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi dissident journalist in the U.S., was murdered inside the
kingdom’s consulate in Istanbul in October 2018. U.S. intelligence agencies later concluded that MBS
had ordered the killing. During his election campaign, Joe Biden had vowed to hold MBS accountable.
Yet, it was Mr. Biden who took steps to rehabilitate the prince. He travelled to Jeddah in July 2022
where he greeted the heir to the Saudi throne with a fist bump. Donald Trump, who brokered the 2020
Abraham Accords, has been keen to deepen America’s traditional ties with its Arab partners. On
Tuesday, he defended MBS’s human rights record, claiming that the prince “knew nothing” about
Khashoggi’s murder. He also promised to sell tanks and F-35 fighters to Saudi Arabia, despite Israel’s
objections. It will also get access to America’s most advanced computer chips. MBS is seeking to build
vast data centres to transform Saudi Arabia into a technological powerhouse.


Historically, Saudi Arabia’s abysmal human rights record has played little role in shaping its
relationship with Washington, long anchored in geopolitical and energy interests. There have been
moments of strain, such as the 1973 oil shock, the post-9/11 distrust or the chill after the Khashoggi
murder, but both sides have consistently prioritised strategic alignment over values. One persistent
complication, however, has been Israel, America’s closest regional ally, which does not have formal
diplomatic ties with Riyadh. After the Abraham Accords were signed, the Biden administration pushed
Saudi Arabia to join the framework by normalising ties with Israel. MBS had said in September 2023
that Saudi Arabia and Israel were in an advanced stage of negotiations. But the October 7 Hamas attack
and Israel’s genocidal Gaza war halted the momentum. Today, Saudi Arabia says it remains open to
joining the Accords, but only if there is a credible, time-bound path towards a two-state solution to the
Palestine question — a position Israel opposes. Mr. Trump appears to have realised both the regional
complexities and Israel’s intransigence. He now seems prepared to deepen ties with Saudi Arabia
without demanding an immediate commitment to recognise Israel. In effect, he has de-hyphenated

Saudi Arabia from the Abraham Accords, for now, choosing instead to cultivate stronger, more direct
ties with the kingdom, which he views as central to his broader West Asia plans.

ties/article70299291.ece

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

Anticipatory bail is a protection granted to a person who has reason to believe that they may be arrested
for a non-bailable offence. It is sought under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, now
re-enacted as Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Unlike regular bail, which
is applied for after arrest, anticipatory bail operates as a pre-arrest safeguard, allowing the person to be
released on bail if and when they are eventually arrested.

A significant question that repeatedly arose before courts was whether anticipatory bail, once granted,
automatically ends when a chargesheet is filed or when the court takes cognizance of the offence. In

February 2026, the Supreme Court settled this question in Sumit v. State of Uttar Pradesh. The Court
held that anticipatory bail, once granted, ordinarily continues without any fixed expiry. The filing of a
chargesheet, the taking of cognizance, or the issuance of summons does not by itself terminate the
protection granted under anticipatory bail, unless the court records special reasons for doing so.

The Court relied on the Constitution Bench decision in Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi),
(2020) 5 SCC 1, which had held that the protection of anticipatory bail should not invariably be limited
to a fixed period and must continue without time restriction unless circumstances change. The Court
also cautioned that courts should not restrict anticipatory bail only up to the filing of the chargesheet as
a matter of course, since such a mechanical approach defeats the purpose of the provision. In the present
case, the Allahabad High Court had granted anticipatory bail restricted to the date of filing of the
chargesheet. When the chargesheet was filed, the protection automatically lapsed, and the appellant's
fresh bail application was rejected. The Supreme Court set aside this approach and held that unless a
court records specific reasons justifying a time limit, anticipatory bail must continue until the end of
the trial.

Being summoned by a Magistrate and required to deposit surety in criminal proceedings
Any kind of coercive action taken by the government under administrative or revenue laws

content.passageText:
In Indian criminal law, an aggrieved person may seek the quashing of a First Information Report (FIR)
by approaching the High Court. Historically, this power was exercised by the High Court either under
Article 226 of the Constitution, which grants the power of judicial review, or under Section 482 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which codifies the High Court's inherent powers to prevent abuse
of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

A key question before courts has been whether the High Court's power to quash an FIR survives after
a chargesheet has been filed and a Magistrate has taken cognizance of the offence. The Supreme Court
addressed this in September 2025, clarifying the position under the new Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha
Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). The Court held that once a chargesheet is filed but before the Magistrate takes
cognizance, a High Court may still quash the FIR and chargesheet under Article 226. However, once
cognizance is taken by the Magistrate, the High Court's power under Article 226 alone is no longer
adequate. At that stage, the petitioner must invoke Section 528 of the BNSS — the equivalent of the
old Section 482 CrPC — and also place the order taking cognizance on record.

The ruling arose because the Bombay High Court had dismissed a quashing petition solely on the
ground that a chargesheet had been filed, treating the petition as infructuous. The Supreme Court found
this approach to be incorrect. The Court observed that where a petition invokes both Article 226 and
Section 528 BNSS, the High Court retains the power to examine the grievance even after cognizance,
provided the necessary documents are on record. Courts have consistently held that the inherent power
to quash is an extraordinary power and must be used sparingly, only in cases where the allegations do
not disclose any offence or where continuation of proceedings would be an abuse of the court's process.

content.passageText:
The right to privacy was not always recognised as a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution.
For several decades, two judgments of the Supreme Court — M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954)
and Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962) — were understood to deny privacy the status of a
fundamental right. This position remained largely unchallenged until the Supreme Court revisited the
question in 2017.

In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court
unanimously declared that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 of the
Constitution, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, and also as part of the freedoms
under Part III. The Court overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise.
The judgment established that privacy encompasses a person's right over their own body, information,
choices, and identity. It is not a mere statutory right that Parliament can take away, but an intrinsic part
of life, liberty, and dignity.

The Court also laid down a three-part test for determining when the State may legitimately restrict the
right to privacy: first, there must be a law authorising the restriction; second, the restriction must serve
a legitimate State interest; and third, the restriction must be proportionate, meaning it must not be more
intrusive than is necessary to achieve the legitimate aim. The judgment had immediate implications for
the Aadhaar scheme, data protection legislation, and surveillance practices. It also recognised that
privacy is not absolute and can be curtailed when the test of legality, legitimacy, and proportionality is
met. The judgment is considered one of the most consequential constitutional rulings of modern India,
placing privacy alongside life and liberty as a core right.

         framers did not include it

That the right to privacy applies only to personal communications and telephone tapping by
         the government

That the right to privacy is a qualified fundamental right subject only to the reasonable
        restrictions in Article 19

Constitution, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, and also as part of the freedoms
under Part III. The Court overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise.
The judgment established that privacy encompasses a person's right over their own body, information,
choices, and identity. It is not a mere statutory right that Parliament can take away, but an intrinsic part
of life, liberty, and dignity.

The Court also laid down a three-part test for determining when the State may legitimately restrict the
right to privacy: first, there must be a law authorising the restriction; second, the restriction must serve
a legitimate State interest; and third, the restriction must be proportionate, meaning it must not be more
intrusive than is necessary to achieve the legitimate aim. The judgment had immediate implications for
the Aadhaar scheme, data protection legislation, and surveillance practices. It also recognised that
privacy is not absolute and can be curtailed when the test of legality, legitimacy, and proportionality is
met. The judgment is considered one of the most consequential constitutional rulings of modern India,
placing privacy alongside life and liberty as a core right.

Article 72 of the Constitution of India vests in the President the power to grant pardons, reprieves,
respites, and remissions of punishment, and to suspend, remit, or commute sentences of persons
convicted of offences. This power may be exercised in three categories of cases: where the punishment
has been imposed by a court-martial; where the offence involves a law to which the executive power of
the Union extends; and in all cases where the sentence is one of death. The pardoning power is one of
the most significant executive powers touching upon the administration of criminal justice.

A pardon is a complete forgiveness of the offence and removes all legal penalties. A commutation
substitutes one form of punishment with a lighter one — for instance, a death sentence may be

commuted to life imprisonment. A remission reduces the quantum of punishment without changing its
nature. A reprieve is a temporary postponement of execution, often sought in death sentence cases. A
respite is the grant of a lighter sentence on account of special circumstances such as pregnancy.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that the President does not exercise this power independently.
In Maru Ram v. Union of India (1981), the Court established that the President must act on the advice
of the Council of Ministers. The President cannot override or ignore ministerial advice, though under
Article 74(1) the President may return the advice for reconsideration once. The power is also subject to
limited judicial review. In Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006), the Court held
that the decision can be challenged if it is arbitrary, mala fide, or based on irrelevant considerations. In
Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014), the Court held that inordinate and unexplained delay in
deciding a mercy petition is itself a ground to commute the death sentence. A similar but more limited
power vests in Governors under Article 161 for offences under state law, but Governors cannot grant
pardon in cases tried by court-martial or in death sentence cases.

content.passageText:
Kidnapping and abduction are two distinct offences under Indian criminal law, now governed by
Sections 137 and 138 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the corresponding
provisions in the Indian Penal Code, 1860. While both offences involve the unlawful removal of a
person from a place, they differ significantly in their essential elements.

Section 137 of the BNS defines two types of kidnapping. The first is kidnapping from India, which
involves transporting a person beyond India's territorial limits without their consent or the consent of a
person legally authorised to give it. The second is kidnapping from lawful guardianship, which involves
taking or enticing a child under 18 years of age, or a person of unsound mind, away from their lawful
guardian without the guardian's consent. Importantly, the offence of kidnapping from lawful
guardianship is complete the moment the child is removed from the guardian's custody. The victim's
consent is entirely irrelevant since a minor is legally incapable of giving valid consent. Kidnapping
from lawful guardianship is not a continuing offence — it is complete once the removal occurs.

Abduction under Section 138 is defined differently. It applies to persons of any age and consists of
compelling a person by force, or inducing a person by deceitful means, to go from any place. Unlike
kidnapping, abduction by itself is not an offence. It becomes punishable only when it is accompanied
by a guilty or wrongful intention, such as abduction for murder, for ransom, or for forced marriage.

Abduction is a continuing offence — it persists as long as the person is being moved. In S. Varadarajan
v. State of Madras (1965), the Supreme Court held that if a minor voluntarily and without enticement
leaves their guardian's custody, it does not constitute kidnapping. The key distinction between the two
offences lies in the age of the victim, the role of consent, and whether the act by itself is an offence or
requires an additional criminal intent.

         hours continuously

         the FIR is filed

         the competent court

At a particle physics laboratory, two standard dice — Die P and Die Q — are used to encode
experimental sequence identifiers. On any standard die, opposite faces always sum to seven: the face-
pairs are 1–6, 2–5, and 3–4. The rolling rules are as follows. Rolling east (rightward): the west face
rises to the top, the top moves to the east face, the east face drops to the bottom, and the bottom moves
to the west face; the south and north faces are unaffected. Rolling north (forward): the south face rises
to the top, the top moves to the north face, the north face drops to the bottom, and the bottom moves to
the south face; the east and west faces are unaffected. Rolling south (backward) is exactly the reverse
of rolling north: the north face rises to the top, the top moves to the south face, the south face drops to
the bottom, and the bottom moves to the north face. Die P is placed in its initial position with face 2 on

top and face 1 on the south (facing the observer); no further orientation information is given for Die P
beyond what these placements and the rolling rules establish. Die Q is placed with face 3 on top and
face 5 on the south. Die P is then rolled two steps forward (north) in succession. After these two rolls,
the face now on top of Die P is identical to the face on the south of Die Q before Die Q is rolled at all.
Die Q is subsequently rolled one step backward (south) followed by one step to the right (east). After
these two rolls, the face now on top of Die Q is identical to the face that was on the north side of Die P
in its original, unrolled position.

content.passageText:
Congestion pricing is charging vehicles a fee to enter designated zones during peak hours, has moved
from a niche transport-economics idea to an increasingly common urban policy tool. London introduced
the world's best-known scheme in 2003, and within a year traffic entering the central zone had fallen
by nearly a third, with the collected revenue directed toward bus and cycling infrastructure. Stockholm
ran a seven-month trial in 2006 before residents, having experienced the reduced congestion and cleaner
air firsthand, voted in a referendum to make the charge permanent. New York followed in January 2025,
becoming the first major American city to price entry into lower Manhattan; early data showed fewer
vehicles crossing into the zone and measurably faster bus speeds along key corridors. Advocates argue
that pricing scarce road space, much like pricing any other scarce resource, is the most efficient way to

allocate it, and that the resulting revenue can fund public transit improvements that benefit far more
residents than the relatively small share who drive into city centres. Critics, however, contend that the
policy is inherently regressive: a flat fee weighs far more heavily on a lower-income delivery driver or
shift worker than on a wealthy commuter, and some drivers, priced out of the zone, simply reroute
through neighbouring untolled streets, displacing rather than eliminating traffic and pollution.
Supporters respond that most schemes now pair the charge with income-based exemptions, discounted
rates for residents, and dedicated reinvestment in bus routes serving lower-income neighbourhoods,
which shifts more of the net benefit toward exactly the population critics worry about. Displacement
effects, they add, tend to shrink once transit alternatives improve and become the more attractive option.
Weighing the evidence from three cities across two decades, the overall case suggests that congestion
pricing, implemented alongside deliberate equity safeguards and transit reinvestment, functions as a
genuinely effective—if still imperfect and contested—tool for managing urban traffic.

options:

          lower-income drivers, regardless of other benefits it might bring.

Paired with equity safeguards and transit reinvestment, congestion pricing is an effective, if
          imperfect, traffic-management tool.

London, Stockholm, and New York all prove conclusively that congestion pricing eliminates
          urban traffic congestion entirely and permanently.

Public referendums of the kind held in Stockholm are a necessary precondition before any city
          can permanently adopt congestion pricing.

the world's best-known scheme in 2003, and within a year traffic entering the central zone had fallen
by nearly a third, with the collected revenue directed toward bus and cycling infrastructure. Stockholm
ran a seven-month trial in 2006 before residents, having experienced the reduced congestion and cleaner
air firsthand, voted in a referendum to make the charge permanent. New York followed in January 2025,
becoming the first major American city to price entry into lower Manhattan; early data showed fewer
vehicles crossing into the zone and measurably faster bus speeds along key corridors. Advocates argue
that pricing scarce road space, much like pricing any other scarce resource, is the most efficient way to

allocate it, and that the resulting revenue can fund public transit improvements that benefit far more
residents than the relatively small share who drive into city centres. Critics, however, contend that the
policy is inherently regressive: a flat fee weighs far more heavily on a lower-income delivery driver or
shift worker than on a wealthy commuter, and some drivers, priced out of the zone, simply reroute
through neighbouring untolled streets, displacing rather than eliminating traffic and pollution.
Supporters respond that most schemes now pair the charge with income-based exemptions, discounted
rates for residents, and dedicated reinvestment in bus routes serving lower-income neighbourhoods,
which shifts more of the net benefit toward exactly the population critics worry about. Displacement
effects, they add, tend to shrink once transit alternatives improve and become the more attractive option.
Weighing the evidence from three cities across two decades, the overall case suggests that congestion
pricing, implemented alongside deliberate equity safeguards and transit reinvestment, functions as a
genuinely effective—if still imperfect and contested—tool for managing urban traffic.

content.passageText:
The world’s oceans absorb approximately a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activity
each year. While this has slowed the pace of atmospheric warming, it has had a less visible but equally
serious consequence: ocean acidification. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic
acid, which lowers the ocean’s pH. Since pre-industrial times, average surface-ocean pH has dropped
from roughly 8.2 to 8.1, a shift that represents a 26 per cent increase in acidity, because pH is measured
on a logarithmic scale. Many ocean organisms including corals, oysters, mussels, and certain plankton
build their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, a compound that dissolves more readily in
acidic conditions. As acidity rises, these organisms struggle to maintain their structures. Coral reefs,
which support an estimated 25 per cent of all marine species, are particularly vulnerable: reef-building
corals grow more slowly in acidified water and recover less effectively from bleaching events caused
by warming temperatures. The effects extend up the food chain. Pteropods, tiny free-floating molluscs
that serve as a critical food source for fish, seabirds, and whales, have already shown shell dissolution
in parts of the Southern Ocean that have crossed acidification thresholds. Unlike many environmental
problems, ocean acidification has no known technical fix. Proposals to add alkaline substances to the
ocean to counteract acidification have been tested only on small scales, and scientists warn of
unpredictable ecological side effects. The only effective long-term solution, researchers agree, is to
reduce carbon dioxide emissions at their source. Until that happens, the chemical transformation of the
world’s oceans will continue unabated, altering ecosystems that hundreds of millions of people depend
on for food and livelihood.

options:

          across the entire Southern Ocean

The absorption of carbon dioxide by the oceans has contributed to an increase in seawater
          acidity since the pre-industrial period

Adding alkaline substances to the ocean is the most effective and widely endorsed solution to
          the problem of acidification

A pH drop from 8.2 to 8.1 represents a ten per cent increase in ocean acidity since the numerical
          difference between the values is 0.1

Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term in office, his administration’s
conduct of foreign policy has been that of a schoolyard bully. This is particularly true in 2026,
when the U.S. launched attacks on two oil-rich countries, Venezuela and Iran. The first was on the
blatantly false pretext of terming President Nicolás Maduro the head of a drug cartel, and the
second was at the instance of Israel. As with schoolyard bullies everywhere, the Trump
administration recognises no rules and mistakes the absence of violent resistance for proof of its
strength. The strangling of Cuba is a case in point. After seizing Venezuela’s energy assets,
abducting its President, and cutting off Venezuelan oil supply to Havana, the U.S. threatened
countries such as Mexico that sought to step into the breach, and imposed a de facto naval blockade
on Cuba, leading to a severe fuel crunch and acute distress for ordinary Cubans. This behaviour,
justified by Mr. Trump as an attempt to take over Cuba and remove its decades-long communist
government, is part of a strategy so nakedly imperial that it has been termed the “Donroe Doctrine”,
a crude play on the original instrument of U.S. hemispheric dominance for over two centuries. Yet,
the bully’s power is often brittle and holds only until someone calls the bluff. When Russia, Cuba’s
ally since the Soviet era, dispatched a tanker, Anatoly Kolodkin, as humanitarian aid to fuel-
starved Cuba, it also tested the will of the Trump administration to interdict a ship owned by
another nuclear power. The tanker reached without incident.


The U.S., it turns out, did not push back and the bluff now stands exposed, even if by a country
that has itself displayed similar behaviour in neighbouring Ukraine. Cuba’s fuel crisis has not
ended and the threat of American attacks still hangs over the socialist government led by President
Miguel Díaz-Canel. But Russia’s timely help reveals that the rest of the world need not simply
endure the Trump era as this administration goes about breaking every accepted tenet of the
international order. For all its flaws as a one-party state, Cuba has been an avowed member of the
Non-Aligned Movement, has shown solidarity with the Global South by deploying well-trained
doctors for medical programmes across poor countries, and has contributed materially to anti-
colonial struggles for decades. It is time other countries repaid the Cubans by showing the will to
break the American blockade and continue sovereign trade and commerce with Cuba, asserting


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


their right to do so. After all, the international order holds only when its constituents accept that
might does not always make right.
SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/a-bully-blinks-on-the-us-and-
cuba/article70807856.ece

         with Russia.

Cuba has been forced to reduce its medical programmes in poor countries due to lack of
         funding.

Cuba is experiencing severe fuel shortages caused by the disruption of Venezuelan oil
         supplies and American threats to potential suppliers.

justified by Mr. Trump as an attempt to take over Cuba and remove its decades-long communist
government, is part of a strategy so nakedly imperial that it has been termed the “Donroe Doctrine”,
a crude play on the original instrument of U.S. hemispheric dominance for over two centuries. Yet,
the bully’s power is often brittle and holds only until someone calls the bluff. When Russia, Cuba’s

another nuclear power. The tanker reached without incident.

endure the Trump era as this administration goes about breaking every accepted tenet of the
international order. For all its flaws as a one-party state, Cuba has been an avowed member of the

Idleness, vice, and intemperance had done their miserable work, and the dead mother lay cold
and still amid her wretched children. She had fallen upon the threshold of her own door in a
drunken fit, and died in the presence of her frightened little ones. Neighbors went hastily to the old
tumble-down hut, in which she had secured little more than a place of shelter from summer heats
and winter cold: some with grave-clothes for a decent interment of the body; and some with food


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


for the half-starving children, three in number. Of these, John, the oldest, a boy of twelve, was a
stout lad, able to earn his living with any farmer. Kate, between ten and eleven, was a bright, active
girl, out of whom something clever might be made, if in good hands; but poor little Maggie, the
youngest, was hopelessly diseased. Two years before a fall from a window had injured her spine,
and she had not been able to leave her bed since, except when lifted in the arms of her mother.


"What is to be done with the children?" That was the chief question now. The dead mother would
go underground, and be forever beyond all care or concern of the villagers. But the children must
not be left to starve. After considering the matter, and talking it over with his wife, farmer Jones
said that he would take John, and do well by him, now that his mother was out of the way; and
Mrs. Ellis, who had been looking out for a bound girl, concluded that it would be charitable in her
to make choice of Katy, even though she was too young to be of much use for several years.


"I could do much better, I know," said Mrs. Ellis; "but as no one seems inclined to take her, I must
act from a sense of duty. I expect to have trouble with the child; for she's an undisciplined thing--
used to having her own way."


But no one said "I'll take Maggie." Pitying glances were cast on her wan and wasted form and
thoughts were troubled on her account. Mothers brought cast-off garments and, removing her
soiled and ragged clothes, dressed her in clean attire. The sad eyes and patient face of the little
one touched many hearts, and even knocked at them for entrance. But none opened to take her in.
Who wanted a bed-ridden child?


"Take her to the poorhouse," said a rough man, of whom the question "What's to be done with
Maggie?" was asked. "Nobody's going to be bothered with her."

It might be difficult to imagine today but just two decades ago, the Maoist movement held large
swathes of central and eastern India in its grip. Roughly a fourth of India’s districts had seen Left-
wing extremism in some form, and chunks of its tribal heartland were under the writ of the
insurgency. Though Naxalism first took root in the north Bengal hills in the 1970s amid simmering
peasant unrest and anxiety about economic inequality, a hungrier and more violent Maoist
ideology had slowly spread across central India in the 1990s, reaching its peak in the 2000s and
2010s. Even after prime minister Manmohan Singh described Maoism as India’s biggest internal
security challenge in 2006, the insurgency only gained in strength, inflicting severe infrastructure
damage and conducting a string of attacks that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of civilians and
security personnel. An ill-advised attempt to create a citizen’s militia against the rebels only ended
up antagonising the tribal population while committing human rights violations.


It is against this grim historical backdrop that the spectacle of Maoism on its last legs looks
impressive. Union home minister Amit Shah on Monday told Parliament that the government had
met its March 31, 2026 deadline to weed out Left-wing extremism in the country, underling this
administration’s tougher, more muscular stance against the insurgent — bullet for bullet. The home
minister rightly praised the government’s efforts to make infrastructure inroads into regions once
deemed impenetrable — erecting mobile phone towers, building roads and markets, and
establishing police outposts. But once the Maoists are wiped out, the government will need to
redouble its efforts, both on security arrangements and civilian administration.


At the heart of the Maoist success was a kernel of discontent among ordinary people who felt
abandoned by the administration, especially in moments of tragedy or disaster. A credible and
transparent civilian administration with fair elections that ensures the active participation of local
communities, must remain high on the agenda of the authorities. This will require a change of
gears — from a muscular securitised approach to a softer, more humane, more democratic one.
Authorities must stay away from heavy handed operations or building local militias; instead they
must bolster law and order. Corruption and apathy — often the bane of civic authorities elsewhere


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


in India — must not be allowed to grow roots. The next phase in the Red Corridor needs a
transformative vision.
SOURCE:https://www.hindustantimes.com/editorials/a-new-sunrise-in-the-red-corridor-
101774969898323.html

It is not for nothing that the head of Art Recovery International has lamented the current “smash
and grab period” of art thievery. The masked men who broke into the Magnani Rocca Foundation
in Italy’s Parma region and made off with three paintings — a Renoir, a Cézanne and a Matisse
— showed little patience for the finesse and style that seem to have characterised such endeavours
in the past. They used a crowbar to force open an entrance and were in and out in under three
minutes.


Gentlemen thieves like Thomas Crown and Arsène Lupin may be mere products of the
imagination, but art history is replete with stories of purloiners who combined their taste for the
rare and beautiful — and the profits they bring — with a sense of mischief and real love for the
art. Take the two Norwegian burglars who stole Edvard Munch’s “The Scream” from the National


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


Museum in Oslo, leaving behind a courteous note: “A thousand thanks for your poor security”. Or
consider the two men dressed as policemen who walked into the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum
in Boston and made the now infamous announcement, “Gentlemen, this is a robbery”, making off
with 13 works.


Then there was Stéphane Breitwieser, art thief extraordinaire who walked off with pieces from
nearly 200 museums — simply because they moved him. No smashed glass, hold-ups or bloodshed
were involved, just good taste and chutzpah. His luck turned in 2001 when his mother, angered by
his criminal behaviour, disposed of his nearly $1.25-billion collection, and Breitwieser was
arrested. The smashers-and-grabbers of today may not execute their crimes with quite the same

India is fast becoming one of the world’s biggest AI user bases. The question now is how it can
turn that scale into superpower status rather than just training Silicon Valley for free. That will be
a tall order for a country largely caught flat-footed by the boom. But let’s start with the basics: The
three main building blocks of AI are talent, compute (including high-end chips and infrastructure)
and data. India doesn’t lack engineers, but it currently lacks foundational research training at scale


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


and sufficient advanced processors in public labs and universities. What it has, in abundance, is
data. It should treat this as a strategic asset rather than leaking it as a free export.


It’s a key reason US Big Tech is making a blitz for the market. With roughly a billion people
online and a massive mobile-first population, India generates a torrent of the kind of human
feedback that makes AI systems better on a daily basis. The world’s most-populous country is the
second-biggest user base of both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude after the US, while
accounting for just a fraction of these platforms’ revenue. The dynamic exposes how much more
the market matters for training purposes right now than making money. These free-to-use services
and promotions aimed at Indian phone users come with a cost. It’s part of a strategic Silicon Valley
grab for Indian languages, voices and behaviours that will make foreign systems smarter first. The
South Asian nation risks repeating a familiar historical pattern of exporting the raw materials for
pennies then buying back imported models at a premium. Meanwhile, it will be left to absorb a job
shock and social impacts at home.


Ultimately, India’s data reckoning should be about who controls this strategic input to AI and who
captures the value from it. The answer isn’t to wall off user outputs from the world. It’s about
finding creative solutions and leveraging them to set rules that reflect what’s actually being
extracted. If its peoples’ data is a key ingredient for building advanced AI, the government should
demand more than apps and marketing in return. It can seek partnerships that build capacity,
including public compute commitments, access to high-end chips, robust training pipelines for AI
researchers, and collaborations that go beyond token commitments.
SOURCE:https://www.livemint.com/opinion/online-views/india-data-trove-ai-majors-free-
access-artificial-intelligence-openai-chatgpt-training-llm-11772345752253.html

content.passageText:
The programme of “non-violent non-cooperation” included the boycott of councils, courts and
schools, set up by the British and of all foreign cloth. With some naivete Gandhi claimed that his
movement was not unconstitutional: in his dictionary, constitutional and moral were synonymous
terms. The British saw that the success of “non-cooperation” would paralyse their administration,
Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, tried to kill with ridicule ‘the most foolish of all foolish schemes”,
which would “bring ruin to those who had any stake in the country”. A number of eminent
“moderate’ politicians joined official critics in underlining the risks of mass non-cooperation as
proposed by Gandhi. That a political programme had no chance of success without an adequate
organization to implement it, Gandhi had realized at the age of twenty-five, when he had founded
the Natal Indian Congress to fight for the rights of Indians in Natal. The Indian National Congress,
had, therefore, to be refashioned, if it was to prove an efficient instrument of non-violent non-
cooperation, Gandhi saw that what the country needed was not a forum for an annual pageant and
feast of oratory, but a militant organization in touch with the masses. Under the new constitution,
the congress was given a broad-based pyramidal structure by formation of village, taluka, district
and provincial committees, with the All India Congress Committee and the Working committee at


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


the apex. The Congress was thus reorganized not only on a more representative basis, but in such
a way that it could function efficiently between its annual sessions. It ceased to be a preserve of
the upper and middle classes; its doors were opened to the masses in the small towns and villages
whose political consciousness Gandhi himself was quickening.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

Consideration turns a bare promise into an enforceable obligation. Section 2(d) of the Indian
Contract Act, 1872 treats any act, abstinence or promise furnished at the desire of the promisor as
sufficient consideration, and Section 25 renders an agreement without consideration void as a
general rule, subject to three carve outs. First, a promise founded on natural love and affection
between parties standing in a near relationship binds the promisor only if the promise is committed
to writing and registered. Second, a promise to compensate a person who has already, on their own
initiative, rendered some service to the promisor may be enforced even though the service preceded
the promise. Third, a written and signed promise to discharge a debt that has become unenforceable


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


through the passage of time will bind the promisor notwithstanding the absence of fresh
consideration.

Distinct from consideration is the rule that only those who are parties to a bargain may sue upon
it. English authority anchored this proposition in a dispute over the resale price of tyres, and Indian
courts, though never codifying the rule in statute, have consistently declined to let outsiders
enforce agreements made for their advantage. Yet courts carve narrow inlets through this wall. A
person named as the object of a trust may compel its performance despite standing outside the
contract that created it. A family settlement drawn up to benefit a relative allows that relative to
insist on its terms even without having signed the settlement. Where a charge is fastened onto
immovable property for the benefit of a third person, that person too may enforce the charge.
Courts have repeatedly cautioned against widening this list further; each addition has demanded
proof that the arrangement was unmistakably designed to confer a direct benefit on the outsider,
and mere incidental advantage will not suffice to displace the general bar against strangers suing
on a contract.

content.passageText:
For over a century, Section 124A of the Penal Code, 1860 punished any act bringing or attempting
to bring the Government of India into hatred, contempt or disaffection, a provision long attacked
as a tool inherited from colonial rule to muzzle dissent. When the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
replaced the Penal Code, the legislature dropped Section 124A in its earlier form and, in its place,
enacted Section 152, which targets acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India,


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


including conduct that excites secession, armed rebellion or subversive activity directed against
the country or its government.

Even before this legislative change, the Supreme Court had already placed the older provision into
abeyance through a 2022 order, directing that no fresh first information reports be registered under
it while its constitutional validity remained pending consideration. That intervention followed
mounting judicial unease that the sweeping language of the older provision was being turned
against journalists, activists and ordinary critics of government policy, persons whose speech
enjoys protection as part of the freedom of expression guaranteed by the Constitution.

Section 152 confines the offence to conduct that actually endangers sovereignty or incites armed
rebellion, expressly carving mere criticism of government out of its reach. Courts have repeatedly
affirmed that pointed criticism of official policy, however severe, does not cross into this offence
unless it tends to incite violence or public disorder, and that tendency must be the proximate, not
merely a remote, cause of any resulting unrest. This recalibrated threshold represents a deliberate
attempt to reconcile the imperatives of national security with the constitutionally guaranteed
liberty to speak freely.

         appeals by organisers to remain peaceful. The editor is charged under Section 152.

Liability follows because severe criticism of governmental functioning naturally
         undermines the unity of the nation.

Liability is unlikely, since the publication incited no violence and showed no proximate
         tendency toward disorder.

Liability follows because a protest that is later accompanied by disorder automatically
         satisfies the statutory threshold.

Liability follows because electoral mobilisation against the ruling government necessarily
         amounts to a subversive activity.

content.passageText:
Part Eighteen of the Constitution equips the President to proclaim a National Emergency under
Article 352 whenever the security of India, or any part of it, is threatened by war, external
aggression or armed rebellion. The last ground replaced the older, more elastic phrase internal
disturbance through the Forty Fourth Amendment of 1978, a change meant to raise the threshold
for invoking this power. Before such a proclamation can issue, the Cabinet must tender its advice
in writing; the proclamation must secure approval from both Houses of Parliament, by a majority


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


of the total membership of each House and not less than two thirds of members present and voting,
within one month; and it may thereafter be revoked whenever the Lok Sabha passes a resolution
to that effect by a simple majority.

A proclaimed emergency reshapes the ordinarily federal distribution of legislative and executive
power. Article 353 permits Parliament to legislate on subjects otherwise reserved to the States, and
allows the Union executive to direct State governments on any matter. Where the proclamation
rests on war or external aggression, Article 358 automatically suspends the freedoms guaranteed
by Article 19 for the emergency's duration. Under Article 359, the President may additionally
suspend, by order, the right of citizens to approach courts for enforcement of other Fundamental
Rights, though this suspending power can never touch Articles 20 and 21, which remain
enforceable throughout.

India has invoked this power three times, in 1962 during hostilities with China, in 1971 during the
conflict with Pakistan, and in 1975 on grounds of internal disturbance, an episode later regarded
as a grave constitutional overreach. The safeguards introduced by the Forty Fourth Amendment,
mandatory written Cabinet advice, a strict one month window for parliamentary ratification, and
revocability by an ordinary Lok Sabha majority, were direct responses to that experience. The
Supreme Court has since clarified, in a 1980 ruling upholding the basic structure against a
sweeping amendment, that courts retain some capacity to examine the validity of an emergency
proclamation, rather than treating it as wholly beyond judicial reach.

Part Eighteen of the Constitution equips the President to proclaim a National Emergency under
Article 352 whenever the security of India, or any part of it, is threatened by war, external
aggression or armed rebellion. The last ground replaced the older, more elastic phrase internal
disturbance through the Forty Fourth Amendment of 1978, a change meant to raise the threshold
for invoking this power. Before such a proclamation can issue, the Cabinet must tender its advice
in writing; the proclamation must secure approval from both Houses of Parliament, by a majority


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


of the total membership of each House and not less than two thirds of members present and voting,
within one month; and it may thereafter be revoked whenever the Lok Sabha passes a resolution
to that effect by a simple majority.

A proclaimed emergency reshapes the ordinarily federal distribution of legislative and executive
power. Article 353 permits Parliament to legislate on subjects otherwise reserved to the States, and
allows the Union executive to direct State governments on any matter. Where the proclamation
rests on war or external aggression, Article 358 automatically suspends the freedoms guaranteed
by Article 19 for the emergency's duration. Under Article 359, the President may additionally
suspend, by order, the right of citizens to approach courts for enforcement of other Fundamental
Rights, though this suspending power can never touch Articles 20 and 21, which remain
enforceable throughout.

India has invoked this power three times, in 1962 during hostilities with China, in 1971 during the
conflict with Pakistan, and in 1975 on grounds of internal disturbance, an episode later regarded
as a grave constitutional overreach. The safeguards introduced by the Forty Fourth Amendment,
mandatory written Cabinet advice, a strict one month window for parliamentary ratification, and
revocability by an ordinary Lok Sabha majority, were direct responses to that experience. The
Supreme Court has since clarified, in a 1980 ruling upholding the basic structure against a
sweeping amendment, that courts retain some capacity to examine the validity of an emergency
proclamation, rather than treating it as wholly beyond judicial reach.

Articles 15(4) and 16(4) of the Constitution permit the State to make special provision for the
advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, and for reservation in public
employment, respectively. A recurring difficulty in implementing these provisions concerns
migration, the situation in which a candidate belonging to a reserved category outperforms the last
selected general category candidate in the final merit list and seeks to be treated as unreserved.
Recruiting authorities have long grappled with whether reservation is merely a floor beneath which
a candidate cannot fall, or whether availing any concession along the way permanently fixes that
candidate within the reserved category.

In January 2026, the Supreme Court addressed this question in the context of the Indian Forest
Service examination. A candidate belonging to a reserved category had cleared the preliminary
screening stage by securing marks below the cut off prescribed for the general category, relying
instead on the relaxed cut off available to her category. Although she went on to outrank several
general category candidates in the final merit list, compiled from the written examination and
interview, the Court held that having entered the selection process through a relaxed standard at
any stage, she could not thereafter be treated as having competed on general standards for the
purpose of allocating an unreserved vacancy.

The Court reasoned that reservation and its accompanying relaxations are policy tools that operate
through the entire selection process rather than being confined to the stage at which they are
availed; a candidate who would not have reached the next stage without the concession cannot
erase that fact through later performance. Whether migration remains open therefore turns on the
specific recruitment rules in force: where those rules impose an express bar on migration after
availing a concession, superior final merit cannot override it, though authorities retain room to
permit migration where their own rules do not impose such a bar.

content.passageText:
The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 embodies a beneficial scheme under which compensation for
accident victims must be just, adequate and calculated to restore the claimant, so far as money can,
to the position enjoyed before the accident. Tribunals compute this compensation under two broad
limbs: pecuniary loss, principally the loss of dependency or of the estate calculated from the
deceased or injured person's income, and non pecuniary loss, comprising conventional heads such
as loss of consortium, loss of estate, and funeral or transportation expenses. The Supreme Court
has periodically standardised these conventional heads to prevent wide disparity between tribunals
awarding compensation for materially similar losses.

Where an injury rather than death is involved, the assessment does not stop at the percentage of
physical disability certified by a medical board. Courts have long distinguished physical disability,
a clinical measurement, from functional disability, which asks how far the injury actually impairs
the claimant's capacity to pursue the specific vocation by which she earned her livelihood. A
claimant whose profession depends on a particular physical capability may suffer a functional loss
far exceeding the certified physical percentage, and tribunals must examine the claimant's
occupation, skill and future prospects rather than mechanically applying the certified figure.

Consortium too has expanded beyond its historical confines. What began as a spouse's claim for
loss of companionship has been read to extend to comparable claims by parents for the loss of a
child's care and by children for the loss of a parent's guidance, each recognised as a distinct
conventional head payable in addition to, and not in substitution for, pecuniary loss. Tribunals
retain a continuing obligation to identify heads of loss that legitimately arise on the facts before
them, even where a particular head was not specifically pressed by the claimant or awarded by the
court below.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 preserves a graded scheme of property offences inherited from
the earlier Penal Code. Theft, defined under Section 303, consists of dishonestly taking movable
property out of another's possession without that person's consent. Two elements are
indispensable: the property must be movable, so that machinery or fixtures become capable of
theft only once severed from the earth, and the taking must be both dishonest and without the
possessor's consent. The offence is complete the moment the property is moved with dishonest
intent, irrespective of whether the offender ultimately succeeds in carrying it away.

Extortion, defined under Section 308, dispenses with the requirement of a surreptitious taking
