During a compliance audit, five subsidiary units: Aurum, Bexley, Corvin, Delmar, and Estry each
submitted a sequence of five quarterly profit figures, in ₹ lakhs, covering Q1 through Q5 of the
same fiscal year. Corvin's sequence follows a constant-ratio geometric rule. Delmar's sequence
follows a rule where the difference between successive terms itself increases by a constant amount
every quarter. Estry's odd-numbered quarters (Q1, Q3, Q5) follow one constant-difference rule,
while its even-numbered quarters (Q2, Q4) follow a separate constant-difference rule, together
forming an alternating pattern. The remaining two units, Aurum and Bexley, follow a plain
constant-difference rule and a perfect-square-based rule, in some order, and the unit following the
perfect-square-based rule reported a Q1 figure of ₹16 lakh. Twice Aurum's common difference
equals Corvin's common ratio multiplied by four, and Aurum's Q1 figure, increased by three times
its own common difference, equals exactly Bexley's Q2 figure. Exactly one figure among all
twenty-five reported values was altered from its true value by a since-dismissed accountant; the
gap between this tampered figure and the true figure the affected unit's rule would have produced
equals Aurum's common difference minus four. Bexley's reported figures for Q1–Q5 are 16, 25,
36, 49, and 64. Corvin's are 6, 18, 54, 162, and 486. Delmar's are 10, 15, 23, 36, and 48. Estry's
are 9, 27, 15, 32, and 21.
content.questionText: Which of the following must be true?
options: Aurum's common difference is smaller than Estry's even-quarter common difference.
Bexley is the unit following the constant-ratio pattern.
Delmar's true Q4 figure is ₹34 lakh, two lakh less than the figure originally reported.
The tampered figure appears in Estry's sequence.

content.passageText:
Every time a person signs up for a new app or website, they are presented with a privacy policy.
In theory, this document explains how their personal data will be collected, stored, and used. In
practice, researchers have found that the average privacy policy takes roughly thirty-four minutes
to read in full, and that most people click “I agree” without reading a single word. This means that
informed consent — the legal and ethical cornerstone of data collection — is, for most users,
entirely fictitious.

The data collected by technology companies is not merely biographical. It includes behavioural
data: which links a person clicks, how long they linger on a page, what they search for at three in
the morning. Aggregated and processed by algorithms, this data produces accurate profiles of a
person’s mental state, political views, purchasing intentions, and even health conditions. These
profiles are then sold to advertisers, insurance companies, and political campaigns, often without
the user’s meaningful awareness.

Defenders of the current system argue that users receive valuable services for free in exchange for
their data, and that anyone who objects can simply choose not to use the platforms. This argument,
critics respond, ignores the reality that opting out is no longer practically possible for most people:
access to jobs, social relationships, and civic participation now depends on digital platforms in
ways that were unimaginable two decades ago.

The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), introduced in 2018,
attempted to address this imbalance by granting users rights to access, correct, and delete their
data. Early assessments suggest it has had a meaningful effect in some areas, particularly in
requiring companies to be more explicit about consent. However, critics note that enforcement has


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


been inconsistent, and that the regulation has not fundamentally altered the business model that
depends on mass data collection.

The deeper problem, some scholars argue, is that data privacy is being treated as an individual
consumer choice when it is, in fact, a collective concern. Your genetic data, for instance, reveals
information about your relatives who never consented to share it. Your social network data
describes your friends. Treating privacy as a personal preference to be traded away ignores the fact
that data about one person always implicates others.

           understand what data is being collected or how it will be used.

Users freely and knowingly exchange their personal data for valuable online services,
           making the existing data collection model both fair and ethically acceptable.

Data privacy cannot be adequately protected by treating it as an individual consumer
           choice, because the current system undermines genuine consent and has collective
           consequences.

content.passageText:
In 2012, scientists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published research describing a
molecular tool called CRISPR-Cas9, which can edit DNA with a precision that earlier techniques
could not achieve. The system works by guiding a protein to a specific location in the genome,
where it cuts the DNA strand, allowing researchers to delete, correct, or insert genetic material. Its
relative simplicity and low cost triggered what many researchers described as a revolution in
biomedical science, and the two scientists were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in
2020.

The medical potential is substantial. Diseases caused by a single faulty gene — such as sickle cell
anaemia and cystic fibrosis — are now realistic targets for CRISPR-based therapies. In 2023, the
United Kingdom became the first country to approve a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease,
offering patients who previously faced a lifetime of painful episodes a potential functional cure.
Clinical trials for several other conditions are underway in multiple countries.

However, the same technology that corrects a faulty gene in an adult patient’s cells can also be
applied to embryos, potentially altering every cell in a future person’s body, including their
reproductive cells — meaning such edits could be inherited by future generations. In 2018, Chinese
scientist He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to edit embryos that were then carried to
term, producing the first gene-edited human babies. The global scientific community’s response
was swift and near-unanimous: the experiment was condemned as premature, unsafe, and ethically
unacceptable, and He Jiankui was subsequently sentenced to prison in China.

Ethicists draw a critical distinction between somatic gene editing — altering cells in a living
patient, with effects confined to that individual — and germline editing, which modifies eggs,
sperm, or embryos and produces heritable changes. Most regulatory bodies consider somatic


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


editing broadly acceptable under appropriate oversight, but view germline editing as posing risks
that have not been adequately addressed. These include unknown off-target effects, the
impossibility of obtaining consent from a future person, and the risk of so-called “designer babies”:
using the technology not only to prevent disease, but to select for traits such as intelligence or
appearance.

Proponents of germline editing argue that if safety concerns can be resolved, there is a moral
obligation to use available tools to eliminate preventable suffering. Critics counter that this logic
could justify an escalating series of enhancements with unpredictable social consequences. The
global scientific community has therefore called for a moratorium on heritable human gene editing
until robust regulatory frameworks are in place. [Extracted with revisions from coverage in Nature,
The Guardian, and MIT Technology Review.]

           future generations.

Somatic editing is more technically complex and expensive than germline editing, which
           is why most researchers prefer germline approaches when treating single-gene disorders
           in clinical settings.

Somatic editing is universally prohibited by international scientific consensus because of
           the unpredictable risk of off-target effects that could seriously harm the patient being
           treated.

Germline editing is considered ethically acceptable by most regulatory bodies because it
           prevents genetic disease at the earliest possible stage, before any individual experiences
           the suffering caused.

molecular tool called CRISPR-Cas9, which can edit DNA with a precision that earlier techniques
could not achieve. The system works by guiding a protein to a specific location in the genome,

biomedical science, and the two scientists were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in
2020.

anaemia and cystic fibrosis — are now realistic targets for CRISPR-based therapies. In 2023, the
United Kingdom became the first country to approve a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease,
offering patients who previously faced a lifetime of painful episodes a potential functional cure.
Clinical trials for several other conditions are underway in multiple countries.

However, the same technology that corrects a faulty gene in an adult patient’s cells can also be
applied to embryos, potentially altering every cell in a future person’s body, including their
reproductive cells — meaning such edits could be inherited by future generations. In 2018, Chinese
scientist He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to edit embryos that were then carried to
term, producing the first gene-edited human babies. The global scientific community’s response
was swift and near-unanimous: the experiment was condemned as premature, unsafe, and ethically
unacceptable, and He Jiankui was subsequently sentenced to prison in China.

DATA INTERPRETATION

India’s smartphone exports, propelled by the Production-Linked Incentive scheme, have climbed
in fits and starts since the programme’s launch. In the very first full year, overseas shipments rose
by three-fifths over the base with which the scheme began. The pace then cooled the next year
considerably, growth slipping to 35 percentage points below that opening-year rate. Momentum
returned the year after, when growth exactly doubled what had been recorded twelve months


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com


earlier, only for the rate to ease again in the most recent year, settling ten percentage points short
of that pace.

Through the two most recent years, Apple-linked contract manufacturers: Foxconn, Pegatron and
the homegrown Tata Electronics have together cornered exactly seven-tenths of the country’s
smartphone export value in each year, leaving the rest to non-Apple brands spearheaded by
Samsung. That non-Apple slice, in the latest year, was worth $3.78 billion. Within the Apple camp,
Tata Electronics supplied 18 per cent of shipments in the year before the latest year; its share has
since climbed by ten percentage points. Samsung’s grip on the non-Apple camp, meanwhile, has
loosened by the same margin from three-quarters of that camp’s shipments down to a share ten
percentage points lower.

Geography tells its own story. Shipments crossing the Pacific to the United States accounted for 5
percentage points more than half of all smartphone exports leaving Indian shores last year. Of
these America-bound consignments, all but fifteen per cent carried an Apple-linked label.

A metallurgical workshop received a contract to manufacture five solid metal components, labelled

shape, and each is cast from molten alloy so that no metal is lost during the casting process.

Component A is a right circular solid cylinder with a base radius of 14 cm and a height of 15 cm.
Component B is a right circular solid cone with a base radius of 7 cm and a height of 24 cm.
Component C is a solid rectangular cuboid whose length, breadth and height are 16 cm, 12 cm and
10 cm, respectively. Component D is a solid hemisphere with a radius of 21 cm. Component E is
a solid sphere whose radius is equal to the radius of Component D.

After the initial casting, the workshop supervisor reworks two pairs of components. First,
Components A and B are completely melted down together, and the molten metal is recast, without
any wastage, into a new solid right circular cylinder of base radius 7 cm. In a separate and unrelated
operation, Component E alone is melted down and recast, without any wastage, into two identical
solid hemispheres; one of these two newly formed hemispheres is then joined, flat face to flat face,
with the original Component D to form one single complete solid sphere.

All original components and newly recast solids are made of the same homogeneous alloy, so the
total volume of metal is conserved in each melting and recasting operation described above. Take
π = 22/7 throughout the passage and the questions that follow, unless stated otherwise.

A metallurgical workshop received a contract to manufacture five solid metal components, labelled
A, B, C, D and E, for use in a hydraulic assembly line. Each component has a distinct geometric
shape, and each is cast from molten alloy so that no metal is lost during the casting process.

Component A is a right circular solid cylinder with a base radius of 14 cm and a height of 15 cm.
Component B is a right circular solid cone with a base radius of 7 cm and a height of 24 cm.
Component C is a solid rectangular cuboid whose length, breadth and height are 16 cm, 12 cm and
10 cm, respectively. Component D is a solid hemisphere with a radius of 21 cm. Component E is
a solid sphere whose radius is equal to the radius of Component D.

After the initial casting, the workshop supervisor reworks two pairs of components. First,
Components A and B are completely melted down together, and the molten metal is recast, without
any wastage, into a new solid right circular cylinder of base radius 7 cm. In a separate and unrelated
operation, Component E alone is melted down and recast, without any wastage, into two identical
solid hemispheres; one of these two newly formed hemispheres is then joined, flat face to flat face,
with the original Component D to form one single complete solid sphere.

total volume of metal is conserved in each melting and recasting operation described above. Take

AI has entered the portals of educational institutions - schools, colleges, universities - at a speed
that makes the entry of computers a generation ago seem glacial. Hrrmphs regarding the danger it
poses as a detour for critical thinking in young minds is less Luddite than those who believed
computers would signal the end of civilisation as we knew it. So, without sounding alarmist,
guidance and policy must keep pace with rapid proliferation of generative AI in education. The
urgency is driven by the fact that tech companies are turning to schools and universities across the
world as potential consumers and clients - apart from the free options already available. In this
case, 'caveat emptor' goes beyond the usual warning.


The aggressive marketing draws on the old playbook of computers to improve computer literacy.
Again, Fomo is driving schools to sign up. For the education system at large, there is no need to
shun this technology. On the contrary, familiarity is necessary to ensure that a new generation
learns new ways of using it. Which is why it's more than helpful to draw on learnings from the old
computer access programmes to develop necessary guidance for teachers, education
administrators, curriculum developers and parents. Training on how to use AI in classrooms and
beyond, as well as a tool to enhance teaching and the learning experience without undermining
efforts to enhance critical thinking, cognitive skills and learning outcomes is essential.


AI's rapid deployment presents a challenge to accurately determine actual learning outcomes and
learning loss. Efforts must be made to disincentivise AI as the option for students to 'outsource'
their learning and learning outcomes. Make it an integral tool, not cheat sheet.

From childhood, I carry a memory both tender and vivid of the gentle clip-clop of tongas outside
railway stations, their worn wooden wheels turning patiently, drawn by horses whose names we
never knew. We would climb aboard as a family, and those slow rides offered a sense of rhythm,
simplicity, and wonder. Recently, that memory came rushing back to me as I saw a photograph
from Gaza. A donkey-drawn cart creaked forward under the weight of a fleeing family: Three
children clinging to their parents, bags of belongings teetering in the back, and the donkey pulling
on, battered and thin.


That image broke me. Not just for what it shows of human suffering, but for the silent resilience
of the donkey, an animal often mocked and neglected, yet carrying the unbearable burdens of war
and its aftermath. The donkey does not speak, does not choose, does not understand the
abstractions in whose name wars are waged. Yet in its mute endurance, it exposes the obscenity


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


of a politics that blesses destruction while speaking the language of security and destiny.
Anonymous and indispensable, the donkey becomes the last symbol of unconditional care and the
innocent voiceless victims in a place where modern systems have collapsed, a silent labourer of
war for whom there is no manger waiting at the end.


In Gaza, the donkey indeed emerges as a silent comrade in the struggle for survival. What
devastates me most is the helplessness of it all. The image of children sitting in the cart, innocent
and wide-eyed, on their way to nowhere. The father walking alongside, powerless to protect them.
The donkey limping on, trying to do what it was never asked to do. And yet, the cart still carries a
strange cosiness. The children huddle together, as if pretending this were just a journey to a picnic,
not exile. The donkey walks, tired but unyielding, as if it, too, is hoping for a warm stable to
welcome him on the other side of misery. In this cold, calculated, and unfeeling world, it is the
cart in Gaza that underscores what dignity looks like in ruins, in movement, in endurance.


Though a relic in a world that worships acceleration, the cart resists the tyranny of haste, moving
not with urgency, but symbolically suggesting the “politics of slowness”. I see a quiet, almost
unbearable dignity in the image of the donkey. In a time when human conscience lies buried
beneath propaganda and spectacle, it is this humble companion that bears the weight of their
survival and the cold, calculated silence of a world that refuses to care.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/in-good-faith-why-the-image-of-a-
donkey-in-gaza-broke-me-10460924/

welcome him on the other side of misery. In this cold, calculated, and unfeeling world, it is the
cart in Gaza that underscores what dignity looks like in ruins, in movement, in endurance.


Though a relic in a world that worships acceleration, the cart resists the tyranny of haste, moving
not with urgency, but symbolically suggesting the “politics of slowness”. I see a quiet, almost
unbearable dignity in the image of the donkey. In a time when human conscience lies buried
beneath propaganda and spectacle, it is this humble companion that bears the weight of their
survival and the cold, calculated silence of a world that refuses to care.

It’s 15 years since venture capitalist Marc Andreessen said, “software is eating the world”, and he
couldn’t have been more right. We have an app for everything now – multiple apps actually. So,
in a nod to Darwin, software has been eating software. Take for example the news that Google’s
Gemini AI models will power Apple’s Siri virtual assistant. This marks the end of a race that
started in 2010 when Google’s Android OS, and Apple, acquired voice command capabilities
almost simultaneously. Amazon’s Alexa and Microsoft’s Cortana were also hot contenders at one
point. But a Gemini-powered Siri in 2026 proves that software matters more than hardware.


Thanks to the Apple deal, Google’s parent Alphabet has cracked the $4tn valuation club, populated
by just one other entity currently – Nvidia. Of course, markets are fickle. Microsoft and Apple
were there, slipped out, and may be back anytime. What matters is value measured in terms of life-
changing impact. And there’s no doubt the world is much more livable thanks to software.

better weather forecasts and market news. Factories are safer, and product quality better, again
thanks to software. Even war is now software’s playfield. Israel’s Lavender targeting system can
identify Hamas operatives; Ukraine’s Op Spider Web was a modern take on the Trojan horse.

for MNCs at our GCCs, and that’s great, but what we need are brands of our own. Our own world-

content.passageText:
Is Greenland next? That’s the big geopolitical question, fanned daily by Trump & Co. He pulled
out the national security imperative on Sunday. On Monday, his homeland security adviser
Stephen Miller said, “Nobody’s going to fight the US militarily over the future of Greenland.” Fair
point. Denmark, which has controlled Greenland for 300 years, isn’t quite the military power it
was when it harassed the Mughals in Bay of Bengal for 50 years in the 17th century. But just
because Danes have only 16,000 soldiers now doesn’t mean Trump should grab Greenland. Yes,
its strategic location, access to Arctic Ocean, rare earths, and probably billions of barrels of oil,
make it irresistible for him. But this is Europe. There’s no fig leaf of drugs and “invasion” by
immigrants this time.


So, a grab – Danes themselves say it would take five choppers at most – would look awfully bad
on Trump’s dossier. Even if he doesn’t care about Nato. Instead, as Trump said last year, “I think
we’re going to get it, one way or the other,” he should try the “other” tack. His old pitch about
investing “billions of dollars” to create new jobs, to make Greenlanders rich, is a good idea. But
since they are almost as rich as Americans in PPP dollar terms, he must sweeten the deal.
Considering that 85% of them earlier opposed absorption by US, Trump should offer all 58,000 of


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


them $1mn per head, plus US citizenship as icing on the cake, payable after they consent in a
referendum. It will cost US just $58bn – a mere 0.15% of $38tn US national debt. Btw, Trump’s
new ballroom, and retrofitting his Qatari Boeing, are likely to cost over $1bn.


This isn’t an outrageous proposal. People change nationality for economic advantage all the time.
Remember, 56% of Greenlanders are keen on independence from Denmark. And Denmark, which
sold its Caribbean colonies to US in 1917, may be less reluctant than it seems. If this offer
persuades Greenlanders, Trump gets Greenland, and there’s no stain of invasion. Let the dollar
talk.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

In a historic first, the Supreme Court of India, in Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine
SC 358), permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment for a patient who had been
in a Persistent Vegetative State (PVS) for thirteen years following a traumatic brain injury
sustained in 2013.

The petitioner's family approached the Court seeking assessment of the appropriateness of
continuing Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH) — a form of artificial nutrition
delivered through a feeding tube — on the basis that it no longer served the patient's best interests.
The bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan held that CANH constitutes a form of
'medical treatment' rather than basic sustenance, as it is a technologically mediated intervention
prescribed and supervised by trained medical professionals. This classification was significant
because it meant CANH could be lawfully withheld or withdrawn under the passive euthanasia
framework.

The Court applied the 'best interests' principle established in Common Cause v. Union of India
(2018), which recognised the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21 of
the Constitution. The 2026 ruling clarified that the best interests test requires decision-makers —
including doctors, medical boards, family members, and courts — to consider what the patient
himself would have wanted if he possessed decision-making capacity, a standard called


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


'substituted judgment'. However, substituted judgment does not operate as an autonomous
standard; the ultimate inquiry remains what course of action serves the patient's best interest.

Active euthanasia — the deliberate taking of life — remains impermissible. The Court redefined
'passive euthanasia' as 'withdrawal or withholding of medical treatment' to remove associated
stigma. It directed AIIMS to admit the patient to its palliative care centre for a supervised and
dignified withdrawal of treatment. It also directed the Union Government to establish Chief
Medical Officer-nominated panels in all districts for Secondary Medical Boards, and urged
Parliament to enact comprehensive end-of-life legislation to fill the existing legislative vacuum.

           withdrawn if it no longer serves the patient's best interests.

On 24 March 2026, the Supreme Court of India in Chinthada Anand v. State of Andhra Pradesh
(2026 SCC OnLine SC 466) authoritatively settled the question of whether a person born into a
Scheduled Caste community who later converts to Christianity can continue to claim Scheduled
Caste status and invoke the protections of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention
of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

The appellant, born into the Madiga community — a Scheduled Caste in Andhra Pradesh — had
converted to Christianity and served as a pastor for over a decade. Following a caste-based
altercation in his village, he filed an FIR under the SC/ST Act. The Andhra Pradesh High Court
quashed the proceedings, holding that his conversion had extinguished his Scheduled Caste status.
The Supreme Court, in a bench of Justices P.K. Mishra and Manmohan, upheld this view.

The Court anchored its reasoning in Clause 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950,
issued under Article 341. Clause 3 states in absolute and unequivocal terms that no person who
professes a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism shall be deemed to be a member
of a Scheduled Caste. This means conversion to Christianity or Islam results in the immediate and
complete loss of SC status, regardless of birth into an SC community or possession of a valid SC
certificate. The Court relied on Punjabrao v. D.P. Meshram (1964) to hold that 'professing' a
religion means making an open, public declaration of faith — the appellant's pastoral role and
decade-long service constituted such a profession.

The Court also reasoned that SC reservations were designed as 'medicine' for the 'disease' of caste-
based discrimination rooted in the Hindu social order. Since Christianity, by its theological
foundations, does not recognise the caste system, a convert can no longer claim to suffer from the
social disabilities the reservation was intended to remedy. A State Government order granting an
SC certificate could not override the presidential order issued under Article 341. The Ranganath


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Mishra Commission and the Balakrishnan Commission have recommended extending SC status
to Dalit Christians and Muslims, but these recommendations have not yet been enacted into law.

content.passageText:
The right to assemble peacefully and without arms, guaranteed under Article 19(1)(b) of the
Constitution of India, is a cornerstone of democratic participation. However, this right is not
absolute. Article 19(3) permits the State to impose 'reasonable restrictions' on this right in the
interests of sovereignty and integrity of India or public order. In a recent ruling, the Supreme Court
clarified that there is no absolute right to protest at a location of one's own choosing.

In the matter concerning a petitioner who sought the right to hold daily protests 'until World War
III ends' at a specific public venue in the capital, the Supreme Court dismissed the petition with
costs of Rs. 50,000, describing the prayer as 'unusual'. The Court reiterated that while the right to
protest is constitutionally protected, it must coexist with the rights of others to use public spaces
and the State's obligation to maintain public order. Restrictions imposed on the location or duration
of a protest must satisfy the test of proportionality — they must be necessary and not excessive in
relation to the purpose sought to be achieved.

The doctrine of proportionality, as developed in Indian constitutional jurisprudence, requires that
any restriction on a fundamental right must: (i) be backed by a valid law; (ii) pursue a legitimate
aim; and (iii) be proportionate to that aim — not more restrictive than necessary. Courts have
struck down blanket prohibitions on all forms of protest in a given area, holding that a total ban is
disproportionate; authorities must explore less restrictive alternatives before imposing an absolute
prohibition.

At the same time, the Supreme Court has recognised that the manner in which a protest is
conducted can be regulated. In Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary (2012), the Court held
that while protesters cannot be forcibly evicted without due process, the administration retains


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


authority to regulate time, place, and manner of protest. Protest at prominent national monuments
or roads carrying essential services can be regulated more strictly. Disruption of public peace or
obstruction of traffic may empower the State to invoke Section 163 BNSS (formerly Section 144
CrPC) to impose temporary prohibitory orders in a specific locality.

           can evaluate its validity.

The restriction must eliminate all risk of public disorder and apply uniformly across the
           country.

The restriction must be backed by a valid law, pursue a legitimate aim such as public
           order, and be proportionate — not more restrictive than necessary.

content.passageText:
Abetment of suicide is a serious criminal offence under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which replicates Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The offence is
non-bailable, cognizable, and triable by a Court of Session. A conviction under Section 108 BNS
may attract imprisonment of up to ten years and a fine. Abetment is defined under Section 45 of
BNS to include instigating a person to commit an act, conspiring to commit an act, and
intentionally aiding the commission of an act.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that proving abetment of suicide requires establishing a
direct or proximate nexus between the accused's conduct and the victim's decision to end their life.
In Abhinav Mohan Delkar v. State of Maharashtra (2025), the Court upheld the quashing of
charges against government officials, reiterating that harassment alone — however severe —
cannot sustain a charge under Section 108 BNS unless there is a conscious, deliberate intention on
the part of the accused to drive the victim to suicide. Casual friction or professional disagreements,
without targeted and deliberate instigation, do not meet this threshold.

The Court has distinguished between two categories of relationships for the purpose of assessing
abetment: those involving sentimental or intimate ties (such as romantic or familial relationships)
and those involving official or professional relationships. A higher evidentiary standard is applied
in the latter. In official relationships, courts examine whether the accused created a situation of
unbearable and targeted harassment with the specific intent of forcing the victim to see no option
but self-destruction. The Delhi High Court in 2026 observed that a mere romantic breakup does
not, by itself, constitute instigation to suicide under Section 108 BNS.

An important related provision is Section 107 BNS, which applies when the victim is a minor, a
person of unsound mind, or a person who is intoxicated — categories considered inherently
vulnerable. Section 107 prescribes harsher punishment than Section 108, including potentially the
death penalty. The courts have cautioned against the mechanical invocation of abetment charges


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


by grieving families or investigative agencies without rigorous scrutiny of the legal elements,
warning that misuse of the provision can cause grave injustice to the accused.
content.questionText:
According to the passage, which of the following is the correct legal standard for
         establishing abetment of suicide under Section 108 BNS?
options:
The prosecution must establish that the accused was present at the location where the
           suicide occurred and failed to intervene.

The prosecution must show that the accused had a motive to see the victim dead, even if
           no direct act of instigation can be proved.

The prosecution must establish a direct or proximate nexus between the accused's conduct
           and the victim's decision to end their life, along with conscious and deliberate intention
           to drive the victim to suicide.

The prosecution need only show that the accused caused the victim emotional distress on
           the day the suicide occurred.

content.passageText:
Abetment of suicide is a serious criminal offence under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which replicates Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The offence is
non-bailable, cognizable, and triable by a Court of Session. A conviction under Section 108 BNS
may attract imprisonment of up to ten years and a fine. Abetment is defined under Section 45 of
BNS to include instigating a person to commit an act, conspiring to commit an act, and
intentionally aiding the commission of an act.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that proving abetment of suicide requires establishing a
direct or proximate nexus between the accused's conduct and the victim's decision to end their life.
In Abhinav Mohan Delkar v. State of Maharashtra (2025), the Court upheld the quashing of
charges against government officials, reiterating that harassment alone — however severe —
cannot sustain a charge under Section 108 BNS unless there is a conscious, deliberate intention on
the part of the accused to drive the victim to suicide. Casual friction or professional disagreements,
without targeted and deliberate instigation, do not meet this threshold.

The Court has distinguished between two categories of relationships for the purpose of assessing
abetment: those involving sentimental or intimate ties (such as romantic or familial relationships)
and those involving official or professional relationships. A higher evidentiary standard is applied
in the latter. In official relationships, courts examine whether the accused created a situation of
unbearable and targeted harassment with the specific intent of forcing the victim to see no option
but self-destruction. The Delhi High Court in 2026 observed that a mere romantic breakup does
not, by itself, constitute instigation to suicide under Section 108 BNS.

An important related provision is Section 107 BNS, which applies when the victim is a minor, a
person of unsound mind, or a person who is intoxicated — categories considered inherently
vulnerable. Section 107 prescribes harsher punishment than Section 108, including potentially the
death penalty. The courts have cautioned against the mechanical invocation of abetment charges

by grieving families or investigative agencies without rigorous scrutiny of the legal elements,

content.passageText:
A contract of indemnity is defined under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as a contract
by which one party — the indemnifier — promises to save the other party — the indemnity-holder
— from loss caused either by the promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person.
This is one of the 'special contracts' recognised under Indian contract law. Section 125 supplements
this framework by specifying the rights of an indemnity-holder acting within the scope of
authority, including the right to recover damages, costs of legal proceedings, and sums paid under
compromise.

The scope of Section 124 is narrower than the English common law conception of indemnity, as
it does not explicitly cover indemnity arising from events such as fires, floods, or Acts of God —
circumstances typically governed by insurance contracts. However, courts have consistently held
that Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive, and equitable principles may be applied to fill gaps
in the law.

A significant question in Indian contract law is whether an indemnity-holder can claim
indemnification before actually suffering a loss. In the landmark case of Gajanan Moreshwar
Parelkar v. Moreshwar Madan Mantri (1942), the Bombay High Court held that when the
indemnity-holder's liability has become absolute — even if not yet discharged — the indemnifier
may be compelled to pay off the claim or place sufficient funds before the court. This principle of
'anticipatory indemnity' departs from the common law position that the indemnified party must
first discharge liability before claiming from the indemnifier.

It is important to distinguish a contract of indemnity from a contract of guarantee under Section
126 of the Act. In a contract of guarantee, there are three parties — the creditor, the principal
debtor, and the surety. The surety's liability is secondary, arising only when the principal debtor
fails to perform. In a contract of indemnity, the indemnifier's liability is primary and independent.
Further, unlike claims for damages under Section 73 of the Act, which require the aggrieved party
to mitigate losses, the indemnity-holder under Section 124 is under no obligation to minimise the
loss before claiming indemnification.

The law of agency, governed primarily by Sections 182 to 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
establishes the legal framework for one person — the agent — to act on behalf of another — the
principal — in dealings with third parties. Section 182 defines an agent as a person employed to
do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third parties. The principal is bound
by the acts of the agent performed within the scope of actual or apparent authority. A contract of
agency may be created expressly, impliedly, by ratification, or by operation of law under the
doctrine of necessity.

One of the most important principles in agency law is that an agent cannot delegate their authority
to another without the express or implied consent of the principal — captured in the maxim
delegatus non potest delegare (a delegate cannot further delegate). However, Section 190 of the
Act carves out exceptions permitting sub-agency or substitution where the nature of the work
necessitates delegation, where trade usage permits it, or where the principal consents either
expressly or by conduct.

The principal is generally liable to third parties for the acts of the agent done within the scope of
apparent or ostensible authority — that is, authority which the principal has, by words or conduct,
represented the agent to possess, even if actual authority is absent. This principle, known as agency
by estoppel, protects innocent third parties who deal with the agent in good faith. However, where
the agent acts entirely outside the scope of authority and commits a fraud for entirely personal
reasons, the principal may escape liability unless the act is closely connected to duties within the
agent's employment.

Agency terminates by agreement, completion of purpose, death or insanity of either party, or by
revocation or renunciation. Section 202 of the Act creates an important exception: agency coupled
with interest — where the agent has a personal stake in the subject matter of the agency — is
irrevocable by the principal, protecting the agent's interests. Upon termination, the agent has a
right to claim remuneration for services already rendered under Section 219, and is also entitled to
a lien over the principal's property lawfully held by the agent for any amount due under Section
221.

The law of agency, governed primarily by Sections 182 to 238 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
establishes the legal framework for one person — the agent — to act on behalf of another — the
principal — in dealings with third parties. Section 182 defines an agent as a person employed to
do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third parties. The principal is bound
by the acts of the agent performed within the scope of actual or apparent authority. A contract of
agency may be created expressly, impliedly, by ratification, or by operation of law under the
doctrine of necessity.

One of the most important principles in agency law is that an agent cannot delegate their authority
to another without the express or implied consent of the principal — captured in the maxim
delegatus non potest delegare (a delegate cannot further delegate). However, Section 190 of the
Act carves out exceptions permitting sub-agency or substitution where the nature of the work
necessitates delegation, where trade usage permits it, or where the principal consents either
expressly or by conduct.

The principal is generally liable to third parties for the acts of the agent done within the scope of
apparent or ostensible authority — that is, authority which the principal has, by words or conduct,
represented the agent to possess, even if actual authority is absent. This principle, known as agency
by estoppel, protects innocent third parties who deal with the agent in good faith. However, where
the agent acts entirely outside the scope of authority and commits a fraud for entirely personal
reasons, the principal may escape liability unless the act is closely connected to duties within the
agent's employment.

Agency terminates by agreement, completion of purpose, death or insanity of either party, or by
revocation or renunciation. Section 202 of the Act creates an important exception: agency coupled
with interest — where the agent has a personal stake in the subject matter of the agency — is
irrevocable by the principal, protecting the agent's interests. Upon termination, the agent has a
right to claim remuneration for services already rendered under Section 219, and is also entitled to
a lien over the principal's property lawfully held by the agent for any amount due under Section
221.

         from the principal on the sale proceeds. The principal suddenly revokes Gopal's authority

           mandates specific performance of all agency agreements.

LOGICAL REASONING

A woodcraft cooperative is preparing a prototype cubical die for a city's annual heritage fair, where
it will be used at a game stall. Each of the die's six faces bears a different cultural motif: Lotus,
Peacock, Diya, Conch, Mandala, and Bell. Before approving the design for mass production, the
stall's coordinator studies three photographs taken by the artisan, each showing the die after it was
repositioned on the workbench.              In the first photograph, the Lotus face is on top, the Conch face
is towards the viewer, and the Peacock face is on the right. In the second photograph, the Mandala
face is on top, the Diya face is towards the viewer, and the Peacock face is on the right. In the third
photograph, the Bell face is on top, the Mandala face is towards the viewer, and the Conch face is
on the right. The coordinator has additionally confirmed two further facts about the prototype.
First, if the face adjacent to both the Lotus face and the Peacock face is the Diya face, then the
Conch face cannot lie directly opposite the Bell face. Second, given that the Conch face is indeed
confirmed not to be opposite the Bell face, the face lying directly opposite the Bell face must be
adjacent to both the Diya face and the Lotus face. The die is a standard cube: each of its six faces
is adjacent to four other faces and lies directly opposite exactly one face, and two faces on directly
opposite sides of a cube can never be seen at the same time in any single photograph.
content.questionText: Which one of the following must be true about the prototype die?
options: The Diya face is directly opposite the Bell face.
The Lotus face is directly opposite the Bell face.
The Peacock face is directly opposite the Bell face.
The Lotus face is directly opposite the Conch face.

were present in the gallery that evening: Arjun, Bina, Chetan, Divya, Esha, and Farid. It is
established that exactly three of the six always tell the truth and the remaining three always lie,
although it is not yet known which three belong to which group. During questioning, each of them
makes exactly one statement. Arjun states that Divya is a truth-teller. Bina states that Arjun is a
liar. Chetan states that Farid is a liar. Divya states that exactly three of the six are liars. Esha states
that if Farid is telling the truth, then Bina and Chetan are of different types, meaning one of them
is truthful and the other is lying. Farid states that if Arjun is telling the truth, then Esha is lying.
Investigators must use these six statements, together with the fact that a truth-teller's statement is
always accurate and a liar's statement is always false, to determine with certainty who belongs to
which group.

options: Bina is a truth-teller.
Arjun is a truth-teller.
Chetan is a truth-teller.
Esha is a truth-teller.

A legal aid caseworker reviewing an old inheritance file discovers that a retired clerk had recorded
a family's relationships using a shorthand symbol code rather than plain language, apparently to
save time while interviewing an elderly claimant. In the code, a line of the form 'P [symbol] Q'

content.passageText:
Vaccination is one of the most effective public health tools ever developed, yet debates about
mandatory immunisation programmes continue to generate controversy. At the heart of these
debates is the concept of herd immunity — the idea that when a sufficiently large proportion of a
population is immune to a disease, the pathogen can no longer spread freely, and even those who
cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns or immunocompromised individuals, are indirectly
protected. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease: measles, which is highly contagious,
requires roughly 95 per cent of the population to be immune, whereas polio requires around 80 per
cent.

Proponents of mandatory vaccination argue that the decision to remain unvaccinated is not a purely
personal one. Because immunity is a collective resource, free-riding — choosing not to vaccinate
while benefiting from the protection others provide — undermines the very system that protects
the most vulnerable. They argue that just as individuals are legally required to pay taxes or stop at
red lights for the collective good, vaccination should be treated as a civic obligation when public
health is at stake.


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Critics of mandatory vaccination, however, raise concerns about bodily autonomy and state
overreach. They argue that compelling individuals to undergo a medical procedure, however safe,
sets a troubling precedent for government intervention in personal health decisions. Some point to
vaccine hesitancy being driven not by genuine ideological objection but by misinformation and
distrust of health authorities — and that mandates may entrench resistance rather than overcome
it.

Public health researchers increasingly suggest that a better approach may lie in targeted incentives,
accessible healthcare, and transparent communication campaigns rather than legal compulsion.
Evidence from several countries shows that high vaccination rates can be achieved voluntarily
when public trust in institutions is strong and access to vaccines is equitable and convenient.
Addressing distrust and reducing access barriers may therefore prove more durable than
enforcement.

[Adapted with revisions from ‘The Ethics of Vaccine Mandates’, The Lancet, and ‘Herd Immunity
Explained’, World Health Organization.]

content.passageText:
Traditional economics assumes that people are rational agents who consistently make decisions in
their own best interests, carefully weighing costs and benefits before acting. Behavioural
economics challenges this assumption. Drawing on decades of research in psychology, it shows
that human decision-making is systematically influenced by cognitive shortcuts, social norms, and
the way choices are presented — none of which feature in the classical model of rational choice.

One of the most widely discussed applications of behavioural economics is ‘nudge theory’,
developed by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. A nudge is any change to the choice environment
— or ‘choice architecture’ — that predictably alters people’s behaviour without restricting their
freedom or changing financial incentives. Classic examples include placing healthier foods at eye
level in a cafeteria, setting pension enrolment as the default option that employees must actively
opt out of rather than opt in to, or displaying a household’s energy consumption alongside that of
its neighbours.

Nudges have achieved measurable results. In the United Kingdom, the Behavioural Insights Team
found that simply adding a line informing taxpayers that most people in their area had already paid
their taxes significantly increased on-time tax compliance. Pension auto-enrolment, introduced in
the UK in 2012, raised the proportion of eligible workers saving for retirement from under 50 per
cent to over 85 per cent within a decade.


Head Office: Plot No.6, Ground Floor, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saket, Saidulajab, New Delhi – 110030   12minutestoclat.com


Critics of nudge theory, however, argue that it is paternalistic — that nudging people towards
‘better’ choices implies that governments or institutions know best, and quietly steers individuals
without their full awareness. Others question whether nudges address root causes: a nudge might
encourage someone to enrol in a pension scheme but does nothing to raise the income from which
they save. Defenders of nudge theory respond that all choice environments contain some design,
and that making that design deliberate and evidence-based is preferable to leaving it to chance or
commercial interest.

[Adapted with revisions from Thaler & Sunstein, Nudge (2008), and ‘The Nudge Unit’, The
Economist.]

          and financial causes of poor decision-making among low-income populations.

          and deliberate choice architecture can achieve meaningful, measurable improvements in
          outcomes.

          important nudge tool available to governments seeking to improve retirement savings.

their own best interests, carefully weighing costs and benefits before acting. Behavioural

opt out of rather than opt in to, or displaying a household’s energy consumption alongside that of

the UK in 2012, raised the proportion of eligible workers saving for retirement from under 50 per
cent to over 85 per cent within a decade.

CURRENT AFFAIRS
NATO is a defensive alliance. Its members are committed to safeguarding the freedom and security
of all Allies, against all threats, from all directions. They do this by maintaining a credible
deterrence and defence posture based on an appropriate mix of nuclear, conventional and missile
defence capabilities, complemented by space and cyber capabilities. In response to the current
security environment, Allies are significantly strengthening the deterrence and defence of the
Alliance as the backbone of their Article 5 commitment to defending each other. NATO faces the
most dangerous security environment since the end of the Cold War. Russia's war of aggression
against Ukraine has shattered peace in Europe and has gravely undermined global security.
Terrorism continues to threaten stability and security across the world. Hostile actions against
Allied countries are accelerating, from cyber attacks to critical infrastructure sabotage,
assassination attempts and disruptions of civil aviation. These actions are part of a coordinated
campaign to destabilise Europe and North America, and weaken the transatlantic Alliance. As
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said repeatedly, “We are not at war, but we are not at
peace either.”

come together, discuss together and set the foundation of working together for a ‘New India’.

Communalism – Quit India!” In this spirit, let us go to www.newindia.in, make the Sankalp take
a pledge to become a Builder of New India. Let us also encourage others to do the same. The text
of the Pledge will be shared by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

Building on the successful implementation of the first phase of the Semicon India Programme
(Semicon 1.0), the Union Cabinet has approved the next phase of Semicon India Programme
(Semicon 2.0) with a fiscal outlay of ₹ 1,27,500 crore to accelerate the development of a robust
and resilient semiconductor ecosystem in India. The semiconductor industry functions through an
extensive global supply chain involving equipment manufacturers, material suppliers, specialty
chemical producers, industrial gas companies, packaging firms and service providers. Semicon 2.0
therefore focuses on ecosystem development rather than only designing and manufacturing chips.
Building on the initial success in chip design, the focus of Semicon 2.0 is to deepen the design
ecosystem. For the strategic sector's requirements, building blocks, such as compute, memory,
power, networking, RF and sensors, have been identified for the design and development of the
semiconductor IPs/Chips/SoCs which will help in designing and developing new systems. For the
commercial sectors, Startups/MSMEs will get seed money (Risk Capital) and IPs/EDA tools
support. To accelerate the momentum, Indian Companies and companies owned by OCIs will also
be allowed to participate. All eligible companies including the startups and MSMEs will get
deployment linked incentives to offset their higher costs of tape-outs.

content.passageText:
A village panchayat decided to construct a boundary wall around the community park before the
onset of the monsoon season, so that newly planted saplings would remain protected from stray
cattle. The panchayat engaged three workers Aman, Bimal and Chetan for the task, each possessing
a markedly different working capacity on account of their age, experience and physical stamina.
Working alone, Aman, being the youngest and most skilled, could complete the wall in 12 days;
Bimal, working alone, would take 15 days; and Chetan, the oldest and relatively slower, working
alone, would require 20 days to finish the same wall.

To speed up construction and manage labour costs, the panchayat devised an unusual work
schedule. On every odd-numbered day, Aman and Bimal worked together on the wall while Chetan
rested. On every even-numbered day, only Chetan worked on the wall while Aman and Bimal
rested. Once the wall was finished, the panchayat had set aside a total wage of ₹48,000 for the
entire project. This amount was to be distributed strictly in proportion to the actual quantity of
work each worker had contributed to the wall.

The panchayat's clerk, who supervised the work every day, did not maintain any tabular chart of
daily progress; instead, he simply recorded, in a handwritten diary, the cumulative proportion of
the wall completed at the end of each day, along with the names of those who had worked that
day. His diary confirms that the alternating schedule was followed strictly and without any
interruption, right from the very first day until the wall stood fully complete.

together on every single day, without any rest days, until the wall was completed.

CURRENT AFFAIRS

India concluded a major long-term uranium-supply agreement in 2026 as part of its attempt to
expand nuclear-power generation and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The agreement was
signed during the Canadian prime minister’s visit to India and marked a significant
improvement in relations between the two countries after a period of diplomatic tension.

Under the agreement, a leading Canadian uranium producer will supply uranium concentrate
to India for use in its civilian nuclear-reactor fleet. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2027
and continue for almost a decade. The arrangement is among India’s largest long-term
nuclear-fuel procurement contracts.

The agreement supports India’s objective of increasing its nuclear-power capacity to 100 GW
by 2047. India presently depends substantially on coal for electricity generation, while its
domestic uranium resources are limited in quantity and quality. Imported uranium can
support the operation of safeguarded civilian reactors while India continues developing its
indigenous three-stage nuclear programme.

India’s ability to participate in international nuclear commerce is closely connected with the
India–United States Civil Nuclear Agreement negotiated during the 2000s. That agreement
led India to separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place designated civilian
facilities under international safeguards.

India subsequently obtained a country-specific waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The
waiver permitted participating countries to engage in civilian nuclear trade with India even
though India had not joined the principal international treaty governing nuclear non-
proliferation.

The 2026 uranium agreement should therefore be understood as an India–Canada supply
arrangement operating within the international nuclear-trade framework made possible by the
earlier India–US civil nuclear initiative.

content.passageText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS

India concluded a major long-term uranium-supply agreement in 2026 as part of its attempt to
expand nuclear-power generation and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The agreement was
signed during the Canadian prime minister’s visit to India and marked a significant
improvement in relations between the two countries after a period of diplomatic tension.

Under the agreement, a leading Canadian uranium producer will supply uranium concentrate
to India for use in its civilian nuclear-reactor fleet. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2027
and continue for almost a decade. The arrangement is among India’s largest long-term
nuclear-fuel procurement contracts.

The agreement supports India’s objective of increasing its nuclear-power capacity to 100 GW
by 2047. India presently depends substantially on coal for electricity generation, while its
domestic uranium resources are limited in quantity and quality. Imported uranium can
support the operation of safeguarded civilian reactors while India continues developing its
indigenous three-stage nuclear programme.

India’s ability to participate in international nuclear commerce is closely connected with the
India–United States Civil Nuclear Agreement negotiated during the 2000s. That agreement
led India to separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place designated civilian
facilities under international safeguards.

India subsequently obtained a country-specific waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The
waiver permitted participating countries to engage in civilian nuclear trade with India even
though India had not joined the principal international treaty governing nuclear non-
proliferation.

The 2026 uranium agreement should therefore be understood as an India–Canada supply
arrangement operating within the international nuclear-trade framework made possible by the
earlier India–US civil nuclear initiative.

Ladakh underwent a significant administrative reorganisation in 2026 when five new districts
were formally notified. The decision increased the number of districts in the Union Territory
from two to seven and was intended to improve governance in geographically remote areas
where residents often travelled considerable distances to access public services.

The creation of the districts had originally been approved by the Union Ministry of Home
Affairs in August 2024. Their territorial boundaries, headquarters and revenue villages were
subsequently finalised, enabling the Ladakh administration to issue the formal notification in
April 2026.

Three of the new districts were carved out of the former territory of Leh district, while two
were created from Kargil district. Each district was provided with a designated headquarters
for its administrative offices. The reorganisation was accompanied by proposals for new
tehsils, sub-tehsils, patwar circles and district-level government posts.

The creation of administrative districts did not automatically create elected representative
bodies in each district. Ladakh initially continued to have only the two Autonomous Hill
Development Councils that existed before the reorganisation. The administration
subsequently announced that the hill-council system would be extended to all seven districts.

The councils are intended to promote democratic decentralisation by giving elected
representatives a role in district-level planning, development and administration. Their
responsibilities include matters relating to land, local infrastructure, agriculture, public health,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                            4


education and the preparation of development plans, subject to the applicable statutory
framework.

The proposal is particularly significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory without a
legislative assembly. Hill councils consequently provide one of the principal mechanisms for
elected local representation. However, they are statutory bodies created under parliamentary
legislation and are different from the autonomous district councils established under the Sixth
Schedule of the Constitution.

Before the additional councils become fully operational, the administration must complete
measures including any necessary statutory amendments, delimitation of territorial
constituencies, notification of council areas and the conduct of elections.

content.passageText:
Protests against the Ken–Betwa River-Linking Project intensified in Madhya Pradesh in
2026, with project-affected families demanding fair compensation, proper rehabilitation,
recognition of forest rights and greater transparency in land acquisition.

The protesters, many of whom belong to the Gond and Kol tribal communities, adopted
several symbolic methods of resistance. These included lying on mock funeral pyres,
standing in water, observing hunger strikes, placing symbolic nooses around their necks and
suspending cooking in affected villages. Women played a prominent role in the
demonstrations.

The July phase of the agitation was organised on the bank of a river near a village in
_________ district. Police subsequently cleared the demonstration site, citing rising water
levels and safety concerns. The protest leader, who had been on an indefinite fast, was moved
to a hospital. Protesters alleged that the police had detained participants, while the authorities
denied making formal arrests.

The project is intended to transfer water from the Ken basin to the Betwa basin through a
dam, tunnel and canal system. The government argues that the project will provide irrigation
and drinking water to the drought-prone Bundelkhand region while also generating
hydroelectric and solar power.

Opponents question the classification of the Ken as a “surplus” river and argue that the
project will submerge forests, displace thousands of families and affect wildlife habitats.
Particular concern has been expressed regarding the submergence and fragmentation of an
important tiger reserve that underwent a successful tiger-reintroduction programme after its
tiger population had disappeared.

The project consists of multiple components implemented in two phases. Its principal
component is a large dam across the Ken River. Other components include barrages and
irrigation projects in the upper Betwa basin.

The controversy illustrates the wider conflict between large infrastructure projects and the
rights of communities dependent on land and forests. It also raises questions regarding
whether environmental compensation and wildlife-management plans can adequately replace
mature natural ecosystems.

People fortunate to have dogs will insist, not even half-jokingly, that their “baby” can
understand every word they utter. Rover can identify his favourite toy, and Moti will run across
rooms when he hears the word “chicken” (or whatever the puppy’s favourite food happens to
be). In essence, many dog parents — like the parents of some human children — insist that
their baby is secretly brilliant. But in at least one sense, pet dogs had it better than human kids.
No dog mom or dad has ever compared their canine companion unfavourably to the
neighbour’s pooch or complained about them being underachievers. The pride in the so-called
intelligence of their pets can be put down to blind affection. That could change.

A study published in Science last week has made global headlines. Researchers found that
Gifted Word Learner dogs can “acquire novel words by overhearing third-party interactions”
in much the same way that human toddlers do. Not only can these genius dogs label hundreds
of items, they can also pick up vocabulary by eavesdropping on human conversations.
Labelling, linguists and behaviourists will rush to clarify, it isn’t the same as language — in all
its grammatical, lexical and metaphorical complexity. But the study does indicate that non-
human animals can learn in the same ways we do, and perhaps carry within them multitudes
we do not yet comprehend.

But in all this talk of meaning and science, language and being, little thought is being given to
poor Rover and Moti. The study, after all, focuses on the rare, “gifted” dogs. Most are still just
a best friend, loving their people unconditionally. Let’s hope that those parents who want their
kids to be toppers and brilliant, who push them to be cutthroat in a dog-eat-dog world, spoil
the dog — even if they couldn’t spare the child

A cruel battle was being fought. The ground was covered with dead and dying men. The air
was hot and stifling. The sun shone down without pity on the wounded soldiers lying in the
blood and dust.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      13


One of these soldiers was a no-ble-man, whom everybody loved for his gen-tle-ness and
kindness. Yet now he was no better off than the poorest man in the field. He had been wounded,
and would die, and he was suffering much with pain and thirst.

When the battle was over, his friends hurried to his aid. A soldier came running with a cup in
his hand.

"Here, Sir Philip," he said, "I have brought you some clear, cool water from the brook. I will
raise your head so that you can drink."

The cup was placed to Sir Philip's lips. How thank-ful-ly he looked at the man who had brought
it! Then his eyes met those of a dying soldier who was lying on the ground close by. The wistful
look in the poor man's face spoke plainer than words.

"Give the water to that man," said Sir Philip quickly, and then, pushing the cup toward him, he
said, "Here, my comrade, take this. Thy need is greater than mine."

What a brave, noble man he was! The name of Sir Philip Sidney will never be forgotten; for it
was the name of a Christian gentleman who always had the good of others in his mind. Was it
any wonder that everybody wept when it was heard that he was dead? It is said, that, on the
day when he was carried to the grave, every eye in the land was filled with tears. Rich and
poor, high and low, all felt that they had lost a friend; all mourned the death of the kindest,
gentlest man that they had ever known.

content.passageText:
Last year, India bought 1.8L electric cars, 77% over 2024. But in terms of overall car sales this
amounted to just 3.8%. Clearly, 10 years of govt incentives and subsidies haven’t convinced
buyers of the advantages of going electric. Two reasons are obvious: range anxiety + inadequate
charging infra, and high prices + limited choice at the lower end. Low sales, by global
standards, aren’t allowing the Indian EV ecosystem to mature. This explains Indian carmakers’
dread of cheap Chinese EVs slipping in via EU after an FTA. But there’s a counterview. Let
EVs of every ilk come in freely and cheaply. Growing EV popularity will automatically spur
growth of charging and servicing infra, which means more jobs. After all, countries that don’t
make any cars at all, like Australia, also have well-developed fuelling and charging networks.


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                         15


This infra boost will serve domestic carmakers too if they raise their technology game with
R&D, like China did.

But to go on pushing domestic EV sales with subsidies and mandates is pointless. For example,
what will Telangana’s plan to make schools induct 25-50% EVs in their vehicle fleets lead to?
Greater burden on parents. Electric buses cost far more than diesel or gas buses, and because
school buses run for only a couple of hours daily, gains on the air-quality front will be minimal.
Far better to focus on city bus fleets that run from morning to night.

EV subsidies, like Delhi’s ₹1L benefit for 27,000 electric cars priced up to ₹25L, are
questionable on several counts. Who gains from them? The rich. Who’s hurt by the revenue
loss? The poor. Those crores are better used to ensure potable water and sewage don’t mix,
right? A Harvard Law School study found subsidies only encourage the rich to buy EVs as their
non-primary vehicles, worsening urban congestion and pollution. Other studies have shown
that when the government subsidises electric cars, manufacturers have no incentive to lower
prices. Without subsidies, they would have to raise prices on their non-EV cars to offset the
discounts they offer on EVs Let the market work, and save public funds for the public.

content.passageText:
The new US ambassador to India Sergio Gor said on Monday that an amicable Indo-US trade
deal is very much in the realm of the possible and even the larger Indo-US partnership continues
to be robust. These pages have always underlined the importance of patiently pursuing
economic and diplomatic dialogue with the US rather than getting distracted by the shrill
rhetoric coming from Washington. Such a policy approach, however, will also have to keep in


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       17


mind the fact that the days of the US being an open export market to even its closest allies are
almost over and the quid pro quo element in such a relationship will be bigger than the past.

In this context, it is extremely important that India cultivate its economic relations with Europe.
It is a large trading block with consumers who have the highest purchasing power anywhere
outside the US, is also feeling the pinch of the about turn in US’s policies, and is also invested
in looking at India as a stakeholder in maintaining a rules-based democratic framework in the
world unlike an increasingly imperialist US or authoritarian China. The more than 14% jump
in Indian exports to Europe in November — to almost $8 billion — is a welcome development
on this front. To be sure, not much should be read into a month’s trade numbers, and it is worth
noting that Indian exports to Europe fell by more than a billion dollars year on year in October.

However, what makes even a short-term reading of Indo-European trade numbers important is
that trade negotiations are still continuing at multiple levels. A successful and mutually
beneficial conclusion of a trade agreement can very well set a new benchmark for democracies
doing trade well.

content.passageText:
LOGICAL REASONING

The cost of prescription medicines has become one of the most contested issues in healthcare
policy. In many high-income countries, a single course of treatment for conditions such as
hepatitis C or certain cancers can cost tens of thousands of dollars — sums that place effective
treatment entirely beyond the reach of uninsured patients and strain public health budgets. The
pharmaceutical industry defends these prices by pointing to the enormous costs of research and
development. Bringing a new drug to market, the industry argues, requires an average
investment of over one billion dollars across a decade or more of trials, with no guarantee of


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                        22


success. Patent protections, which grant companies exclusive rights to manufacture and sell a
drug for up to twenty years, are therefore presented as essential incentives that make this
investment worthwhile.       Critics challenge this narrative on several grounds. Many
breakthrough medicines, they note, were developed with substantial public funding — through
government grants, university research, and publicly financed clinical trials. If taxpayers bear
a significant share of development costs, the argument goes, they should not then face
unaffordable prices for the resulting medicines. Furthermore, independent analyses have found
that pharmaceutical companies typically spend more on marketing than on research, which
calls into question whether high prices are truly driven by R&D costs or by profit maximisation.
A further complication is that patent protections, while incentivising innovation,
simultaneously block the entry of cheaper generic alternatives. Countries that have issued
compulsory licences — allowing domestic manufacturers to produce generic versions of
patented drugs during public health emergencies — have dramatically reduced medicine costs
without demonstrably harming long-run innovation rates. This suggests that the relationship
between patent protection and pharmaceutical innovation is not as straightforward as the
industry claims. The debate ultimately turns on competing values: the right of companies to
profit from their investments, and the right of patients to access medicines they need to survive.
Neither of these claims is trivial, and any workable solution will require negotiated compromise
rather than the victory of one side over the other.

         development is funded by taxpayers rather than by companies themselves.

         requires negotiated compromise rather than a decisive win for either side.

content.passageText:
Few energy debates generate as much disagreement as the question of whether nuclear power
should play a central role in the transition away from fossil fuels. Proponents argue that nuclear
energy is one of the only proven sources capable of delivering large quantities of reliable, low-
carbon electricity around the clock, regardless of weather conditions. Unlike solar and wind,
which generate power intermittently, nuclear plants operate continuously at high capacity,
making them well-suited to serving as a stable backbone of a decarbonised grid. Supporters
also note that, measured in deaths per unit of energy produced, nuclear power has a safety
record considerably better than coal, oil, or even natural gas. Opponents raise a cluster of
concerns. The first is cost: recent nuclear projects in Western Europe and North America have
run catastrophically over budget and behind schedule, raising questions about whether the
industry can still build plants efficiently. The second is waste: spent nuclear fuel remains
dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, and no country has yet opened a permanent
geological repository for its long-term storage. The third is risk: though catastrophic accidents
are rare, incidents at Chernobyl and Fukushima demonstrated that when things go wrong, the
consequences can be severe, long-lasting, and geographically widespread. Advocates respond
that cost overruns reflect regulatory burdens and construction inexperience that could be
reduced with standardised designs and reformed permitting processes. On waste, they point out
that the total volume of spent nuclear fuel accumulated globally over decades is surprisingly

should play a central role in the transition away from fossil fuels. Proponents argue that nuclear

geological repository for its long-term storage. The third is risk: though catastrophic accidents
are rare, incidents at Chernobyl and Fukushima demonstrated that when things go wrong, the
consequences can be severe, long-lasting, and geographically widespread. Advocates respond
that cost overruns reflect regulatory burdens and construction inexperience that could be
reduced with standardised designs and reformed permitting processes. On waste, they point out
that the total volume of spent nuclear fuel accumulated globally over decades is surprisingly
small. On safety, they argue that the statistical death toll from continued fossil fuel use dwarfs
the historical toll from nuclear accidents. The balance of evidence suggests that dismissing
nuclear power entirely in the name of climate action may be self-defeating. Whether new
reactor designs and streamlined construction can make it economically competitive again is the

Ila, aged eleven, urgently requires a kidney transplant, and the transplant unit at a metropolitan
hospital is evaluating six of her relatives as potential living donors: Om, Priya, Kavita, Naveen,
Rohan, and Sameer. Hospital protocol permits a living-donor transplant without a special ethics
dispensation only when the donor is a parent, child, sibling, grandparent, or grandchild of the
recipient; a relative connected to the recipient solely through marriage requires such a
dispensation regardless of how closely that relative is otherwise connected to the family, even
where the blood relative linking them is very close. The committee's case file, compiled from


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                         28


interviews rather than official records, establishes the following. Priya is Kavita's mother.
Naveen is Priya's son and Kavita's brother. Om is Priya's spouse, and the hospital's caseworkers
apply the standing convention that a person's spouse's children are also that person's own
children. Rohan, who shares no blood relationship with either Om or Priya, is a parent of Ila,
together with exactly one of Om, Priya, Kavita, or Naveen, whichever of the four turns out to
be Ila's other parent. Sameer is Naveen's son. Om, Naveen, Rohan, and Sameer are male; Priya,
Kavita, and Ila are female. Ila's mother has at least one sibling among the six relatives named
above. The committee's file separately leaves two facts undetermined: whether Kavita or
Naveen was born first, and whether Ila or Sameer was born first.
