content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

The freedom to carry on trade, business, occupation or profession under clause (1)(g) of Article
19 protects engagement in games in which skill predominates over chance, since such games
have long been treated as a legitimate commercial activity rather than gambling. This
protection, however, does not extend to betting or wagering, an activity classified as res extra
commercium, meaning it stands wholly outside the constitutional guarantee of trade and cannot
be claimed as a matter of right, however substantial the underlying skill.

Once a stake, being money or property staked upon an uncertain outcome, is introduced into
the play of any game, the activity acquires the character of betting notwithstanding that the
game itself, considered without the wager, would ordinarily be recognised as one of skill; the
relevant enquiry thereupon ceases to be whether skill predominates over chance and becomes
instead whether a stake was risked on the result.

A State Legislature is accordingly competent under Entry 34 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
to prohibit, and not merely regulate, betting connected with any game, including a game that
would otherwise qualify for constitutional protection, since the constitutional immunity
historically extended to skill-based play is a legislative choice rather than a compulsion binding
future legislatures. Independently of Entry 34, a prohibitory enactment may also be sustained
under the public order head in Entry 1, provided the State places before the court empirical
material, such as a dedicated committee's findings on addiction, indebtedness or self-harm
attributable to staked play, establishing a proximate rather than a remote nexus between the
impugned activity and public tranquility; absent such material, reliance on Entry 1 alone would
not suffice.

Mere migration of an already-protected skill-based game from a physical to an online format
does not, by itself, alter its essential character or strip it of protection, for it is the presence of
a stake, and not the medium through which the game is played, that determines whether the
activity falls outside the shelter of Article 19(1)(g).

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

The freedom to carry on trade, business, occupation or profession under clause (1)(g) of Article
19 protects engagement in games in which skill predominates over chance, since such games
have long been treated as a legitimate commercial activity rather than gambling. This
protection, however, does not extend to betting or wagering, an activity classified as res extra
commercium, meaning it stands wholly outside the constitutional guarantee of trade and cannot
be claimed as a matter of right, however substantial the underlying skill.

Once a stake, being money or property staked upon an uncertain outcome, is introduced into
the play of any game, the activity acquires the character of betting notwithstanding that the
game itself, considered without the wager, would ordinarily be recognised as one of skill; the
relevant enquiry thereupon ceases to be whether skill predominates over chance and becomes
instead whether a stake was risked on the result.

A State Legislature is accordingly competent under Entry 34 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
to prohibit, and not merely regulate, betting connected with any game, including a game that
would otherwise qualify for constitutional protection, since the constitutional immunity
historically extended to skill-based play is a legislative choice rather than a compulsion binding
future legislatures. Independently of Entry 34, a prohibitory enactment may also be sustained
under the public order head in Entry 1, provided the State places before the court empirical
material, such as a dedicated committee's findings on addiction, indebtedness or self-harm
attributable to staked play, establishing a proximate rather than a remote nexus between the
impugned activity and public tranquility; absent such material, reliance on Entry 1 alone would
not suffice.

Mere migration of an already-protected skill-based game from a physical to an online format
does not, by itself, alter its essential character or strip it of protection, for it is the presence of
a stake, and not the medium through which the game is played, that determines whether the
activity falls outside the shelter of Article 19(1)(g).
content.questionText:
A State enacts a law prohibiting only online rummy played for stakes, while an identical
     physical, stakes-based version of rummy conducted at licensed gaming clubs within the
     State remains entirely unregulated under any other law. A gaming company argues that,
     because it is the presence of a stake rather than the medium of play that renders an
     activity betting, the State's selective targeting of only the online version is legislatively
     incoherent and therefore invalid. Does the reasoning above support the company's
     argument that the online-only prohibition is incoherent?
options:
Yes, because taxing only one medium while permitting an identical staked activity in
      another medium necessarily amounts to unconstitutional discrimination between
      similarly situated persons.

No, because the reasoning shows only that a stake, not the medium, marks betting; it
      implies no duty to prohibit every instance a legislature may competently reach.

Yes, because a legislature that fails to prohibit an activity in one medium is thereby
      estopped from prohibiting the same activity in any other medium.

No, because physical gaming clubs are licensed establishments and therefore fall
      outside the legislative competence conferred by the betting and gambling entry
      altogether.

content.passageText:
Chapter V of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 imposes obligations styled 'certain relations
resembling those created by contract' upon persons who have received a benefit at another's
expense, even where no agreement, offer or acceptance ever passed between them; liability
rests not upon consent but upon the equitable principle that no person ought to be enriched
unjustly at the cost of another.

Where necessaries suited to the condition in life of a person incapable of contracting, or of any
dependant whom such person is legally bound to support, are supplied to that incapable person,
the supplier is entitled to be reimbursed out of the property of the incapable person; no personal
liability attaches to the incapable person, and recourse lies solely against his estate, if any.

Where a person, though lawfully doing something for another or delivering something to
another, does not intend to act gratuitously, and the other person accepts and enjoys the benefit
of the act or the thing so delivered, the latter is bound to compensate the former or to restore
the thing so delivered; this obligation, however, does not arise merely because a benefit has in
fact accrued, for it presupposes both that the actor did not intend gratuity and that the recipient
had a genuine opportunity to decline the benefit before it was thrust upon him, since a person
who enjoys a benefit conferred without any real choice in the matter incurs no obligation to
compensate.

Separately, a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake, whether
of law or of fact, or under coercion, is bound to repay or return it, this obligation being
unaffected by whether the payer's mistaken belief concerned a question of fact or a question of


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                             39


law, a distinction that carries no weight under the statute notwithstanding its historical
significance in other legal systems.
content.questionText:
A shopkeeper supplies medicines and food, suited to her condition in life, to a minor
      orphan living alone after her guardian's death, at a time when no property whatsoever
      stands in the minor's name. Two years later, the minor inherits a house from a distant
      relative who dies intestate. The shopkeeper, having never been paid, now seeks
      reimbursement for the value of the necessaries supplied, out of the minor's newly
      inherited house. Can the shopkeeper claim reimbursement from the house the minor later
      inherited?
options:
No, because the minor had no property whatsoever at the time the necessaries were
       supplied, and reimbursement fastens only on property owned at that precise moment.

No, because reimbursement requires personal liability on the part of the incapable
       person, which a minor can never incur regardless of subsequently acquired property.

Yes, because the minor's subsequent inheritance converts her into a person capable of
       contracting, thereby exposing her to ordinary personal contractual liability
       retrospectively.

Yes, because reimbursement is secured generally from the incapable person's property,
       without confining its source to property owned precisely when the necessaries were
       supplied.

A painter, acting on his own initiative and without the owner's knowledge, paints the
      exterior of the owner's house while the owner is abroad for a month; the owner returns
      to find the work completed and enjoys its improved appearance. During the same visit
      home, the painter also repaints the boundary fence, this time while the owner stands
      nearby, watches the entire process from start to finish, and says nothing to stop it. For
      which of the two jobs, if any, does the relevant provision entitle the painter to
      compensation?
options:
Only the fence, because the owner's presence and silent acquiescence gave him a
       genuine opportunity to object that he never exercised, unlike the house.

Only the house, because completed work enjoyed after the fact always obliges the
       beneficiary to pay, regardless of whether he had any chance to object beforehand.


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                       40

Both jobs, because the painter never intended either act as a gratuitous gift, and that
      intention alone is sufficient to found an obligation to compensate.

Neither job, because a painter who acts entirely on his own initiative, without being
      asked to paint anything, can never claim compensation under this provision.

content.questionText:
B discovers that A has genuinely evaded certain dues owed to a public authority. B tells
     A that unless A pays him a sum of money, B will report the evasion to the authority
     concerned, an act B is fully entitled to perform. Apprehensive of the consequences such
     a report might bring, A pays the demanded sum. A subsequently seeks to recover the
     payment, asserting that it was made under coercion within the meaning of the passage
     above. Applying the passage's framework, is A's payment recoverable as one made under
     coercion?
options:
Yes, because any payment induced by apprehension of adverse consequences, however
      lawful the threatened conduct, is necessarily a payment made under coercion.

No, because a threat to do something the threatening party is legally entitled to do is
      not coercion, even where the threat induces the payment.

Yes, because B's demand for money in exchange for silence about a genuine violation
      is itself an independently unlawful act, rendering the resulting payment coerced.

No, because the relevant provision excludes from its scope every payment connected,
      however indirectly, to the discovery of a genuine wrongdoing by the payer.

X, a person of unsound mind, has a minor daughter whom X is legally bound to maintain.
     A shopkeeper supplies school books and clothing, suited to the daughter's needs, directly
     to the daughter, without X's knowledge, while X is confined in a care facility. On the
     same day, the same shopkeeper also delivers, entirely unsolicited, an expensive painting
     to X's house purely as a promotional gift, intending no charge whatsoever for it. From
     which of these two supplies, if either, can the shopkeeper claim reimbursement from X's
     property?
options:
Only the painting, because unsolicited gifts delivered to a person's residence
      automatically create a right to reimbursement once the recipient exercises any dominion
      over them.


                                 12minutestoclat.com                                       41

Neither supply, because reimbursement from an incapable person's property requires
       proof that the supply was expressly authorised in advance by that person or a lawful
       guardian.

Only the books and clothing, since they were necessaries supplied to a dependant X
       must support, whereas the painting was expressly meant as a gift.

Both supplies, because everything delivered to a person legally incapable of managing
       his own affairs is recoverable from that person's property as a matter of course.

A firm pays its supplier three separate amounts on the same day: first, an excess sum
      caused by a clerical miscount of units delivered; second, a sum paid in the mistaken
      belief that a tax provision, since struck down eighteen months earlier, still obliged the
      firm to pay it; and third, a discretionary bonus paid with full knowledge of all relevant
      facts and law, intended by the firm purely as a gift with no expectation of return.
      Applying the passage above, which of these three payments is or are recoverable?
options:
Only the first, because recovery for a mistaken payment presupposes discovery within
       a reasonably short time of payment, a condition met only by the clerical miscount.

Only the second, because a deliberate gift made with full knowledge of all facts and
       law is not, by definition, a mistaken payment at all.

The first and third, because mistakes of fact are recoverable without limit while a gift,
       once enjoyed by its recipient, becomes recoverable after a fixed period.

The first and second, since the provision draws no distinction between mistakes of fact
       and law, while a deliberate, fully informed gift is not a mistaken payment.

content.passageText:
The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 was enacted to secure
the welfare, maintenance and protection of the life and property of senior citizens, and one
provision obliges the State Government to frame a comprehensive action plan toward that end;
this provision, being facilitative rather than adjudicatory in character, confers no power upon
the District Magistrate or any other authority constituted under the Act to determine disputed
questions of ownership, or to pronounce upon the validity of a will, gift or conveyance, since
such determinations properly belong to a court exercising ordinary civil jurisdiction upon
regular pleadings, discovery and cross-examination.

By way of a distinct and narrower exception, a separate provision empowers the Tribunal
constituted under the Act to treat a transfer of property made by a senior citizen, whether by


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                       42


way of gift or otherwise, as void, but only where three conditions are cumulatively satisfied:
first, that the transfer was made by a senior citizen; second, that the transfer was made subject
to the condition that the transferee would provide the transferor with basic amenities and basic
physical needs; and third, that the transferee has thereafter failed or refused to provide the same.

Where even one of these three conditions is wanting, whether because no such condition was
attached to the transfer at all, or because the failure to provide amenities cannot be shown, the
Tribunal's jurisdiction under this exception does not arise, and the dispute, however framed,
falls to be agitated before the competent civil court in the ordinary course.

The bar upon the jurisdiction of civil and revenue courts found elsewhere in the Act extends
only to matters that squarely fall within the four corners of this narrow exception and cannot
be read as ousting civil jurisdiction over property disputes lying outside that compass; nor can
a writ court, in the exercise of its supervisory jurisdiction, confer upon the Tribunal an
adjudicatory power that the statute itself withholds.
content.questionText:
An 82-year-old widow gifts her flat to her nephew by a registered deed that expressly
       records the gift as being made in consideration of the nephew agreeing to provide her
       food, medical care and a place to live for the rest of her natural life. Six months later,
       the nephew evicts her without providing any of these things. The widow approaches the
       Tribunal under the Act seeking a declaration voiding the gift deed. Does the Tribunal
       have jurisdiction to declare the gift deed void on these facts?
options:
Yes, because all three elements are satisfied: a senior citizen's transfer, a recorded
       condition of basic amenities, and the transferee's subsequent failure to provide them.

No, because a registered gift deed can only be challenged before the sub-registrar who
       registered it, and never before a statutory Tribunal of this kind.

Yes, because any transfer by a person above sixty years of age is automatically voidable
       at that person's option regardless of its terms or conditions.

No, because a reference to future care is merely a moral expectation unless framed as
       an express condition of the transfer, which this deed does not do.

A senior citizen's son sells inherited agricultural land to a private buyer through a
       registered, wholly unconditional sale deed containing no reference whatsoever to future
       maintenance or care of any kind. Years later, the senior citizen, now visibly frail and
       elderly, alleges the sale deed is a forgery and that his signature upon it was fabricated,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                           43


      and approaches the Tribunal under the Act seeking a declaration that the sale deed is
      void and of no legal effect. Can the Tribunal validly entertain and decide this claim?
options:
Yes, because any senior citizen alleging forgery of a document affecting his property
      may invoke the Tribunal's jurisdiction irrespective of the deed's terms.

No, because the deed records no condition of amenities, so this forgery dispute falls
      outside the narrow exception and must be pursued before a competent civil court.

Yes, because forgery, once alleged by a senior citizen, converts any transfer into one
      automatically covered by the Tribunal's protective jurisdiction under the Act.

No, because allegations of forgery can only be raised in a criminal complaint and never
      form the basis of any civil or tribunal proceeding.

A 75-year-old man living alone has an ongoing boundary dispute with his next-door
      neighbour, an unrelated stranger, over a shared wall. No question of maintenance, gift
      or conditional transfer arises between them at all. The man files a writ petition asking
      the High Court to direct the District Magistrate to adjudicate and resolve the boundary
      dispute under the Act's action-plan provision, since the Magistrate is duty-bound to
      protect senior citizens' property. Should the writ court issue the mandamus sought?
options:
Yes, because the District Magistrate's duty to protect senior citizens' property under the
      action plan necessarily includes resolving any property dispute a senior citizen brings
      before him.

Yes, because a writ court's supervisory power under Article 226 permits it to confer
      adjudicatory jurisdiction on any authority whenever that appears just and convenient.

No, because the action-plan provision is facilitative rather than adjudicatory, confers no
      power to decide boundary or title disputes, and a writ court cannot expand that
      jurisdiction.

No, because boundary disputes between neighbours are non-justiciable altogether and
      cannot be entertained by any court, tribunal or authority under Indian law.

content.passageText:
An act does not amount to an offence if the person doing it was, at the time of doing it,
incapable, by reason of unsoundness of mind, either of knowing the nature of the act, or of
knowing that the act was wrong or contrary to law; either species of incapacity suffices
independently, and an accused is not required to establish both.

The law begins with a presumption that every person is of sound mind and accountable for his
acts, so that the burden of displacing this presumption rests upon the accused, who need only
establish unsoundness of the requisite degree on a preponderance of probabilities, a materially
lighter standard than the prosecution's own burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.


                                  12minutestoclat.com                                          45


The unsoundness relied upon must be shown to have existed precisely at the moment the act
was committed; evidence of insanity before or after that moment, including a subsequent lucid
interval or a prior history of psychiatric illness, is admissible only as material from which the
state of mind at the crucial moment may be inferred, and is never, by itself, conclusive of
incapacity at that moment.

A distinction of central importance separates legal insanity, as defined above, from medical
insanity in the wider psychiatric sense; a person suffering from a diagnosed mental disorder
may nonetheless remain fully liable if, notwithstanding the disorder, he retained the capacity
to know the nature of his act or its wrongfulness, whereas a person free of any diagnosable
disorder but who satisfies the statutory test is entitled to the exemption. Equally, an impulse
that the accused found irresistible, or an act done in extreme passion, does not attract this
exemption where the accused's cognitive faculties remained intact and he knew both what he
was doing and that it was wrong; the statute exempts incapacity to know, not mere incapacity
to resist.

During a psychotic episode, an accused stabs a stranger to death, aware that he is
       physically stabbing a human being with a knife and that this would cause death; owing
       to a delusion, however, he genuinely believes the victim is a supernatural entity that
       must be destroyed to save his family, and he honestly believes this act righteous and
       lawful, not wrongful in any sense. He remains aware, throughout, of exactly what he is
       physically doing. Can the accused successfully invoke the exemption described in the
       passage?


                                       12minutestoclat.com                                    46
options:
No, because full awareness of the physical nature of the act, including that it would
      cause death, is by itself sufficient to defeat the exemption entirely.

No, because the exemption requires the accused to lack awareness of both the act's
      nature and its wrongfulness together, and only the first is absent here.

Yes, because the exemption is satisfied independently through incapacity to know the
      act was wrong, which the delusion here establishes despite his physical awareness.

Yes, but only if a subsequent psychiatric examination establishes a diagnosed disorder,
      since a delusion alone, without formal diagnosis, can never satisfy either limb of the
      exemption.

An accused, charged with culpable homicide, offers no evidence whatsoever of his
     mental state at the moment of the killing, but establishes through hospital records that,
     eleven days after the act, he was admitted in an acutely psychotic state requiring
     emergency sedation. No witness describes his conduct, speech or demeanour during the
     killing itself or in the days immediately preceding it. The defence argues this
     hospitalisation record alone discharges its burden on a preponderance of probabilities.
     Does the hospitalisation record, standing alone, discharge the accused's burden?
options:
Yes, because any medically documented psychiatric episode occurring within a
      reasonably proximate period after an alleged offence conclusively establishes
      unsoundness at the time of the act.

No, because the preponderance of probabilities standard applies only to the prosecution,
      and an accused pleading this exemption must instead disprove guilt beyond reasonable
      doubt.

Yes, because the burden on an accused pleading this exemption is satisfied by producing
      any medical evidence whatsoever, irrespective of its temporal proximity to the act.

This is doubtful, since later unsoundness only evidences the state of mind at the act's
      time, and alone may not establish incapacity at that moment.

A man with a long-documented history of a compulsive disorder assaults a colleague
     after an argument. He later testifies, and psychiatric evidence confirms, that at the
     moment of the assault he fully understood that striking his colleague was both physically
     harmful and legally wrong, but that his compulsive disorder rendered him unable to


                                 12minutestoclat.com                                        47


       restrain the urge to strike out once provoked, however hard he tried to control himself.
       Can this accused successfully invoke the exemption described in the passage?
options:
No, because his cognitive faculties and knowledge of wrongfulness remained fully
       intact, and the exemption addresses incapacity to know, not mere incapacity to resist an
       urge.

Yes, because any medically documented compulsive disorder that overpowers a
       person's self-control is treated as equivalent to unsoundness of mind for every legal
       purpose.

No, because compulsive disorders are, as a class, entirely fictitious conditions not
       recognised by the standard applied under this exemption.

Yes, because the disjunctive structure of the exemption permits either an inability to
       know the act's nature or an inability to control one's conduct to suffice.

       commits an act of grievous violence while suffering an episode of delirium caused by a

content.passageText:
An adjudicatory determination that rests, even in part, upon fictitious, non-existent or
hallucinated judicial precedents, whether such material takes the form of a citation to a
judgment that was never delivered or a paragraph fabricated and wrongly attributed to a
genuine reported decision, is no decision in the eyes of law and must be set aside in its entirety,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                          48


for the introduction of such material contaminates the very process of adjudication rather than
merely one strand of its reasoning.

Significantly, this consequence follows irrespective of whether the fabricated material had a
direct or an indirect bearing upon the ultimate conclusion reached; the vitiating effect does not
depend upon the party impugning the decision demonstrating that the outcome would have
been different had the fictitious material been excluded, and even an iota of such material
occurring anywhere within the decision-making process suffices to taint the whole, a
considerably more exacting standard than the ordinary requirement, familiar elsewhere in
administrative law, that prejudice to the outcome be affirmatively shown before a decision is
disturbed.

The source from which the fabricated material entered the record is immaterial to this
consequence: it is of no relevance to the question of vitiation whether the fictitious citation was
placed before the adjudicating body by a party's counsel or was instead introduced through the
adjudicating body's own independent research, since the taint attaches to the decision itself and
not merely to the conduct of the person who introduced the material.

Distinctly, the question of individual professional accountability turns upon a duty of
verification: an advocate who cites a judgment without having verified its existence and
accuracy commits misconduct, and a judge who relies upon such unverified material without
independent verification commits an equally serious lapse, obligations that are breached by the
failure to verify rather than by the mere act of citation as such.
content.questionText:
A tribunal's order relies on four genuine precedents and one additional citation that turns
       out to be entirely fabricated, attributed to a case that never existed. The party who
       benefited from the order argues that the four genuine precedents, considered alone,
       independently and adequately support the same conclusion, so the fabricated citation
       made no difference whatsoever to the outcome, and the order should accordingly be
       allowed to stand unset aside. Should the presence of adequate independent support from
       genuine precedents save the order from being set aside?
options:
Yes, because a decision is vitiated only where the fabricated material was indispensable
       to the outcome reached, a condition absent here given four genuine precedents.

Yes, because courts must always prefer preserving a substantively correct outcome over
       the formal exercise of setting aside and remanding a matter for fresh consideration.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                          49

No, because vitiation follows once any fabricated material enters the decision-making
      process at all, regardless of whether the outcome would have been identical without it.

No, but only because four genuine precedents are, as a matter of settled practice, treated
      as an insufficient number to independently sustain any conclusion.

content.questionText:
An advocate, before filing written submissions, checks a purported citation against
      what she reasonably believes to be a reputable online legal database, which displays
      what appears to be a complete, correctly formatted judgment. Unknown to her, the
      database entry was itself corrupted by a technical error and the case does not exist. She
      cites it in good faith, having taken this verification step. The tribunal's resulting order is
      later found to rest partly on this fabricated citation. Under the passage's framework, does
      the advocate's good-faith verification attempt affect the two distinct consequences that
      follow?
options:
It affects both consequences identically, since good-faith verification simultaneously
      validates the underlying citation and shields the resulting order from being set aside.

It affects neither consequence, since good faith is wholly irrelevant both to whether the
      order is vitiated and to whether the advocate has committed misconduct.

It affects only whether the order is vitiated, since a good-faith verification attempt
      converts an otherwise fabricated citation into a genuine one for that purpose.

It affects only the misconduct question, since the order stays vitiated regardless of
      intent, while a genuine verification attempt bears on whether she failed that duty.

Following a finding that its earlier order rested partly on a fabricated citation, a
     tribunal's matter is remanded for fresh adjudication. The very same members who
     authored the original, vitiated order are assigned to hear the remanded matter afresh. A
     party objects, arguing that the passage's reasoning requires the remanded matter to be
     heard by an entirely differently constituted bench, since the original members have
     already been exposed to the fabricated material once before. Does the passage's
     reasoning support the party's objection to the same bench hearing the remand?
options:
Yes, because any adjudicator once exposed to fabricated material is conclusively
      presumed incapable of deciding the same matter afresh without continuing bias.

No, because the reasoning requires only that fresh adjudication proceed uninfluenced
      by the vitiated findings; it says nothing about the bench's required composition.

Yes, because reassignment to a differently constituted bench is the sole safeguard
      capable of curing a decision founded on hallucinated material.

No, because a tribunal's composition, once fixed for a matter, can never be altered for
      any reason once proceedings have begun.

occurring anywhere within the decision-making process suffices to taint the whole, a
considerably more exacting standard than the ordinary requirement, familiar elsewhere in
administrative law, that prejudice to the outcome be affirmatively shown before a decision is
disturbed.

consequence: it is of no relevance to the question of vitiation whether the fictitious citation was
placed before the adjudicating body by a party's counsel or was instead introduced through the
adjudicating body's own independent research, since the taint attaches to the decision itself and
not merely to the conduct of the person who introduced the material.

Distinctly, the question of individual professional accountability turns upon a duty of
verification: an advocate who cites a judgment without having verified its existence and
accuracy commits misconduct, and a judge who relies upon such unverified material without
independent verification commits an equally serious lapse, obligations that are breached by the
failure to verify rather than by the mere act of citation as such.

Section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002 renders void any agreement between enterprises that
causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India.
Agreements among enterprises engaged at the same stage of production or trade, such as
arrangements to fix prices, limit or control output, allocate markets or customers, or rig bids,
are presumed to cause such an adverse effect, and this presumption may be displaced only
where the enterprises establish that the arrangement constitutes a joint venture that increases
efficiency in production, supply, distribution or control of goods or services.

Agreements between enterprises operating at different stages of the same production or
distribution chain, including exclusive supply obligations, exclusive distribution arrangements,
refusal to deal and resale price maintenance, attract no such presumption; their legality is
instead tested under a rule of reason, requiring an affirmative demonstration of appreciable
adverse effect having regard to factors including barriers to new entry, foreclosure of existing
competitors and any countervailing benefit accruing to consumers.

Separately, Section 4 prohibits not dominance as such, which is lawful and indeed the natural
consequence of legitimate commercial success, but only the abuse of a dominant position once
such dominance is established. Establishing abuse accordingly proceeds in two distinct stages:
first, the relevant market, defined along both product and geographic dimensions, must be
delineated and the enterprise's dominance within that market ascertained with reference to
market share, countervailing buying power and entry barriers, none of which is by itself a
conclusive numerical threshold; and only thereafter does the enquiry turn to whether the
dominant enterprise's conduct amounts to an abuse of that established dominance.

Conduct identical in form, such as an exclusive supply obligation, may accordingly fall to be
examined either under the rule of reason applicable to vertical agreements or under the abuse-
of-dominance framework, depending entirely on whether the enterprise imposing it is shown
to hold a dominant position in the relevant market.

     applicable to horizontal agreements. Does this arrangement qualify for the joint-venture
     exception described in the passage?

Yes, because any arrangement voluntarily labelled a joint venture by its participants is
      conclusively entitled to the exception, regardless of its actual operation.

Yes, because sharing even one production facility, however nominal, automatically
      satisfies the efficiency requirement attached to the joint-venture exception.

No, because joint ventures between direct competitors are, without exception,

      described.

     clearly defined relevant market, having grown this share entirely through superior
     product quality and organic customer preference. No evidence is placed on record of
     predatory pricing, denial of market access, discriminatory conditions, or leveraging into
     any other market. A competitor argues that this seventy percent share, by itself,
     establishes a contravention of the framework governing abuse of dominant position. Is
     the competitor's argument, that the market share alone establishes a contravention,

I. The National Crime Records Bureau’s annual reports on crime and prison statistics have to
be read with a strong caveat — most of the numbers cannot be compared between States
because they are largely dependent upon the registration/reporting of crimes in the first place.
However, certain national trends and sharp year-on-year changes within States can still reveal
meaningful patterns that could demand policy intervention. The recent NCRB report for 2023
— delayed by a year — points to a worrying trend of postponed surveys, reports and even the
Census under the current Union Government. But there are also three telling numbers: the 2.8%
decrease in murder cases across the country; a staggering 28.8% surge in crimes against
Scheduled Tribes (ST), and a 31.2% increase in cyber crimes. While the decrease in murder
cases will come as a relief to law enforcement — most of the cases pertain to disputes, personal
vendetta or enmity and “gain” — the other two numbers are alarming. The steep rise in crimes
against STs is largely due to the ethnic violence in Manipur, with the registered numbers
jumping from just one in 2022 to 3,399 in 2023 — which a more effective government could
have mitigated. Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan also recorded significantly high crime rates
against tribals, suggesting their vulnerability in the central Indian States. This is not a new
phenomenon; previous NCRB reports have highlighted higher crime rates in regions with
significant tribal populations.

With greater Internet penetration across the country, there has been an increase in
cybercrime, particularly related to financial fraud and sexual exploitation. Anecdotally, it is
evident that these numbers must have gone up even further in the last two years with the
greater use of digital financial instruments in daily transactions and investment. While
policing has tried to keep up with the growing menace of cybercrime, with specialised cells,
the ubiquitousness and deepening spread of digital crimes require more sophistication and
dedication by the police to tackle them. Crimes against children rose by 9.2% in 2023 — with
the offender known to the victim in 96% of the cases. While the increase could be a function
of improved reporting across States, the high number (1,77,335 cases) suggests that States
must work on a war footing to sensitise children about these crimes and inappropriate
behaviour by adults. A subset of these crimes could also include the application of the
POCSO Act in the case of consensual adolescent relationships and this is an area that needs
to be carefully handled by the prosecuting and policing agencies. Reported crimes against
women registered a modest increase of 0.4%, but this masks a 14.9% spike in dowry-related
crimes, pointing to a persistent societal problem.

SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/crime-patterns-on-the-national-crime-
records-bureaus-report-for-2023/article70148719.ece
content.questionText:
If the information above is correct, which of the following is most strongly supported
      about the relationship between digital financial instruments and cybercrime?
options:
The expansion of digital financial transactions has likely contributed to a sustained
      increase in cybercrime beyond what the 2023 NCRB report captures.

Cybercrime rates have remained relatively stable despite the proliferation of digital
      financial instruments in everyday transactions.

The specialized police cells established to combat cybercrime have successfully
      prevented any significant rise in digital financial fraud.

The 31.2% increase in cybercrime is primarily attributable to sexual exploitation
      rather than financial fraud.

decrease in murder cases across the country; a staggering 28.8% surge in crimes against

vendetta or enmity and “gain” — the other two numbers are alarming. The steep rise in crimes
against STs is largely due to the ethnic violence in Manipur, with the registered numbers
jumping from just one in 2022 to 3,399 in 2023 — which a more effective government could
have mitigated. Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan also recorded significantly high crime rates
against tribals, suggesting their vulnerability in the central Indian States. This is not a new
phenomenon; previous NCRB reports have highlighted higher crime rates in regions with
significant tribal populations.

cybercrime, particularly related to financial fraud and sexual exploitation. Anecdotally, it is
evident that these numbers must have gone up even further in the last two years with the
greater use of digital financial instruments in daily transactions and investment. While
policing has tried to keep up with the growing menace of cybercrime, with specialised cells,
the ubiquitousness and deepening spread of digital crimes require more sophistication and
dedication by the police to tackle them. Crimes against children rose by 9.2% in 2023 — with
the offender known to the victim in 96% of the cases. While the increase could be a function
of improved reporting across States, the high number (1,77,335 cases) suggests that States
must work on a war footing to sensitise children about these crimes and inappropriate
behaviour by adults. A subset of these crimes could also include the application of the
POCSO Act in the case of consensual adolescent relationships and this is an area that needs
to be carefully handled by the prosecuting and policing agencies. Reported crimes against
women registered a modest increase of 0.4%, but this masks a 14.9% spike in dowry-related
crimes, pointing to a persistent societal problem.

II. I was to see my old friend, Simon Radevin, of whom I had lost sight for fifteen years. At
one time he was my most intimate friend, the friend who knows one's thoughts, with whom
one passes long, quiet, happy evenings, to whom one tells one's secret love affairs, and who
seems to draw out those rare, ingenious, delicate thoughts born of that sympathy that gives a
sense of repose. For years we had scarcely been separated. Then he married. He married, quite
suddenly, a little girl from the provinces, who had come to Paris in search of a husband.

What would he be like when I met him again? Still lively, witty, light- hearted and enthusiastic,
or in a state of mental torpor induced by provincial life? A man may change greatly in the
course of fifteen years!

The train stopped at a small station, and as I got out of the carriage, a stout, a very stout man
with red cheeks and a big stomach rushed up to me with open arms, exclaiming: "George!" I
embraced him, but I had not recognized him, and then I said, in astonishment: "By Jove! You
have not grown thin!" And he replied with a laugh:

"What did you expect? Good living, a good table and good nights! Eating and sleeping, that
is my existence!"

I looked at him closely, trying to discover in that broad face the features I held so dear. His
eyes alone had not changed, but I no longer saw the same expression in them. Yet his eyes
were bright, full of happiness and friendship, but they had not that clear, intelligent expression
which shows as much as words the brightness of the intellect. Suddenly he said:

"Here are my two eldest children." A girl of fourteen, who was almost a woman, and a boy of
thirteen, in the dress of a boy from a Lycee, came forward in a hesitating and awkward manner,
and I said in a low voice: "Are they yours?" "Of course they are," he replied, laughing. "How
many have you?" "Five! There are three more at home."

I got into a carriage which he drove himself, and we set off through the town, a dull, sleepy,
gloomy town where nothing was moving in the streets except a few dogs and two or three
maidservants. Here and there a shopkeeper, standing at his door, took off his hat, and Simon
returned his salute and told me the man's name; no doubt to show me that he knew all the
inhabitants personally, and the thought struck me that he was thinking of becoming a candidate
for the Chamber of Deputies, that dream of all those who bury themselves in the provinces.

III. Nine years after Cyrus Mistry was unceremoniously removed as chairman of Tata Sons,
and a year after the death of the patriarch, Ratan Tata, the shadow of both still looms over the
storied group. Long held as an exemplar in corporate governance, the group is now a house in
disorder. Sharp differences of opinion have emerged between the trustees of the Tata Trusts,
which together hold roughly 66 per cent stake in Tata Sons, the group’s holding company.
Considering the sheer breadth of sectors it operates in — from steel to auto, software, retail
and semiconductors — another power struggle at the conglomerate could have far-reaching


ramifications. Uncertainty at the top and a long-drawn-out conflict will impact decision-
making, affecting not only the group’s businesses but the wider economy as well.

Reports suggest that the disagreements between the trustees arose over board appointments,
access to sensitive information and the listing of Tata Sons. The RBI had classified Tata Sons
as an upper-layer NBFC and given it a deadline of September 30, 2025 for listing. But, with
the deadline passing — Tata Sons has moved to deregister as an NBFC — the central bank is
still deliberating. A few days ago, Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, vice chairman Venu
Srinivasan, trustee Darius Khambata and Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran met with
Home Minister Amit Shah and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. While government
intervention in the matter would raise a red flag, the fact that the trustees held a meeting with
senior Union government ministers underlines the seriousness of the situation.

The absence of a towering figure following Ratan Tata's death is being felt. Unlike the West,
capitalism in India has tended to be more promoter-driven. For all their limitations, promoters
do tend to bring stability to a business. But the history of the Indian corporate sector is also
littered with examples of how, when strong promoters have passed away or did not have a clear
succession line, the group either weakened or split. Under Ratan Tata’s stewardship, the Tatas
sailed through storms, with an approach that prized achieving “consensus and unanimity on
issues”, as Vijay Singh, who was on the board of Tata Sons, told this newspaper. For a group
that has prided itself on its principled approach to business and has long been held in high
regard for its integrity, this saga must be quickly brought to an end. The Tata Trusts must put
their house in order — it’s vital to their future.

must-put-their-house-in-order-10297941/

III. Nine years after Cyrus Mistry was unceremoniously removed as chairman of Tata Sons,
and a year after the death of the patriarch, Ratan Tata, the shadow of both still looms over the
storied group. Long held as an exemplar in corporate governance, the group is now a house in
disorder. Sharp differences of opinion have emerged between the trustees of the Tata Trusts,
which together hold roughly 66 per cent stake in Tata Sons, the group’s holding company.
Considering the sheer breadth of sectors it operates in — from steel to auto, software, retail
and semiconductors — another power struggle at the conglomerate could have far-reaching


ramifications. Uncertainty at the top and a long-drawn-out conflict will impact decision-
making, affecting not only the group’s businesses but the wider economy as well.

Reports suggest that the disagreements between the trustees arose over board appointments,
access to sensitive information and the listing of Tata Sons. The RBI had classified Tata Sons
as an upper-layer NBFC and given it a deadline of September 30, 2025 for listing. But, with
the deadline passing — Tata Sons has moved to deregister as an NBFC — the central bank is
still deliberating. A few days ago, Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, vice chairman Venu
Srinivasan, trustee Darius Khambata and Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran met with
Home Minister Amit Shah and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. While government
intervention in the matter would raise a red flag, the fact that the trustees held a meeting with
senior Union government ministers underlines the seriousness of the situation.

The absence of a towering figure following Ratan Tata's death is being felt. Unlike the West,
capitalism in India has tended to be more promoter-driven. For all their limitations, promoters
do tend to bring stability to a business. But the history of the Indian corporate sector is also
littered with examples of how, when strong promoters have passed away or did not have a clear
succession line, the group either weakened or split. Under Ratan Tata’s stewardship, the Tatas
sailed through storms, with an approach that prized achieving “consensus and unanimity on
issues”, as Vijay Singh, who was on the board of Tata Sons, told this newspaper. For a group
that has prided itself on its principled approach to business and has long been held in high
regard for its integrity, this saga must be quickly brought to an end. The Tata Trusts must put
their house in order — it’s vital to their future.

IV. According to the caste survey conducted by the Bihar government in 2023, the state had
130.7 million people spread across 27.6 million households. Only about 2 million people held
government jobs in the state, according to the data, some of which were central government
jobs. Now, if Tejashwi is to keep his promise, the state will have to increase the number of
government jobs by a factor of almost 13, which, in turn, will increase the government’s salary
bill by a similar multiple. In 2025-26, Bihar’s salary expenditure is budgeted at ₹54,697 crore.
This number multiplied by 13 would exceed ₹7,00,000 crore. This is more than twice the total
budgeted spending of Bihar in 2025-26, which is ₹3,16,895 crore. To be sure, this is an
underestimate of the spending involved since pensions have not been counted here.

Money is not the only problem here. Unless one is talking about really low-paying government
jobs, where the trend has been to outsource to private providers, Bihar will find it difficult to
find people to hire. According to the 2024 calendar year Periodic Labour Force Survey data,
the share of graduates in Bihar’s 18-35-year-old labour force — the population working or
looking for a job — was just 12.9%, almost half of the national average (23%). The short point
is that Bihar neither has the money nor the skilled workforce to roll out what seems to be
Yadav’s promise of utopian managerial socialism. The promise is so bizarre that it seems the
announcement is not based on even some bare minimum diligence within the party.


One can dismiss it as election rhetoric — the RJD is not the only party to make outlandish
promises during an election campaign — or think of it as a sign of the intellectual bankruptcy
of the primary pole of political opposition in one of India’s most populous and economically
backward states. To be sure, the current government has not exactly changed the state’s
fortunes. Democracy, in its ideal form, should not be vulgar sloganeering to animate a mass of
precarity. It should be driven by a genuine urge to make people’s lives better by making
considered and informed policies. Promises such as providing a government job to every
household in Bihar are an unfortunate reminder that it is mostly the former variety of
democracy that is still around in our country.

101760108472886.html

V. Were it not for the tragic circumstances of his death, Y Puran Kumar would have been
seen as an example of social mobility and of the upholding of the Indian Constitution’s
promise of equality. He was a Scheduled Caste (SC) Indian Police Service officer of the
Haryana cadre; his wife, Amneet P Kumar, is an SC IAS officer, and his brother-in-law is an
MLA in Punjab. On the face of it, Kumar and his family had reached the upper echelons of
government and politics. His suicide and the eight-page note he leaves behind, which alleges
systemic discrimination, including by senior IPS officers, however, casts a shadow on that
image. It also raises disturbing questions about entrenched biases that cramp and distort
institutional spaces. These questions must be addressed, not evaded.

The allegations of “mental and administrative torture” and “caste-based discrimination,
public humiliation, targeted mental harassment and atrocities” by senior officers in Haryana
in Kumar’s dying declaration must be probed. The National Commission for Scheduled
Castes (NCSC) has directed the Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, Chandigarh,
to submit an action taken report in seven days. The state government and police must
investigate Kumar’s suicide urgently, in a transparent manner. The temptation to close ranks
in the face of public and judicial scrutiny must be avoided. Issues of embedded prejudice and
discrimination and their effect on the mental health of those at the receiving end are too
important to be brushed under the carpet. This must be a moment for the police to reflect and
introspect.

Caste is a proven fact in crime and punishment in India. The Status of Policing in India
Report (2025) by Common Cause and Lokniti found that victims of torture are “most often
from marginalised communities” and that police personnel across states see certain SC and
ST communities as “criminal”. The survey also found that “one in every four Scheduled
Caste (SC) police personnel think that Dalits do not get justice”. The caste-based, and even
casteist, nature of policing in India is an unfortunate remnant of a colonial structure that
urgently needs to be consigned to the past. Doing so, however, is easier said than done, and
requires police forces — particularly at the leadership level — to be open and sensitive as
they turn the searchlight inwards. Kumar’s death and his allegations must not be swept under
the institutional carpet. The Haryana police cannot allow discrimination to go unchecked and


unpunished within.

SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/in-haryana-death-of-a-
policeman-and-questions-of-impunity-10300025/

image. It also raises disturbing questions about entrenched biases that cramp and distort
institutional spaces. These questions must be addressed, not evaded.

The allegations of “mental and administrative torture” and “caste-based discrimination,
public humiliation, targeted mental harassment and atrocities” by senior officers in Haryana
in Kumar’s dying declaration must be probed. The National Commission for Scheduled
Castes (NCSC) has directed the Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, Chandigarh,
to submit an action taken report in seven days. The state government and police must
investigate Kumar’s suicide urgently, in a transparent manner. The temptation to close ranks
in the face of public and judicial scrutiny must be avoided. Issues of embedded prejudice and
discrimination and their effect on the mental health of those at the receiving end are too
important to be brushed under the carpet. This must be a moment for the police to reflect and
introspect.

urgently needs to be consigned to the past. Doing so, however, is easier said than done, and
requires police forces — particularly at the leadership level — to be open and sensitive as
they turn the searchlight inwards. Kumar’s death and his allegations must not be swept under
the institutional carpet. The Haryana police cannot allow discrimination to go unchecked and

LEGAL REASONING

XI. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) in India has traditionally been understood as a
statutory obligation requiring companies to allocate a portion of their profits towards social
welfare activities such as education, healthcare, and poverty alleviation. However, the Supreme
Court’s observations in the Great Indian Bustard case have expanded this understanding by
foregrounding environmental responsibility as an inseparable component of CSR. The Court
emphasised that environmental protection cannot be treated as a discretionary or peripheral
activity, especially for corporations whose operations directly or indirectly impact ecological
systems. The case arose in the context of the alarming decline of the Great Indian Bustard, an
endangered species whose habitat overlaps with areas of renewable energy infrastructure and
industrial development. While acknowledging the importance of economic growth and clean
energy transitions, the Court stressed that development cannot proceed at the cost of
irreversible ecological damage. It held that corporate entities, particularly large infrastructure
and energy companies, cannot externalise environmental costs while complying only formally
with CSR spending requirements. The Court linked CSR obligations to constitutional
principles, especially Articles 21, 48A, and 51A(g), which together impose duties on both the
State and citizens to protect and improve the environment. It reasoned that CSR must reflect
these constitutional values and operate as a mechanism of substantive responsibility, not mere
financial contribution. Accordingly, corporate responsibility extends beyond writing cheques
to actively mitigating environmental harm, adopting sustainable practices, and participating in
conservation efforts relevant to their operational footprint. Importantly, the Court clarified that
environmental responsibility under CSR is not limited to compensatory measures after damage
has occurred. Preventive and precautionary actions are equally crucial. The judgment thus
signals a shift from a narrow, compliance-driven model of CSR to a purposive, impact-oriented
framework. In this framework, corporations are expected to internalise environmental costs
and align their business strategies with long-term ecological sustainability, rather than treating
CSR as an isolated statutory checkbox.

ecosystem-prevent-species-extinction-supreme-court/article70416803.ece, 20-12-2025

       financial contribution.

The company may still be non-compliant because environmental responsibility is an
       integral part of CSR.
The company’s actions are lawful as long as the environmental harm is unintentional.
Both A and C.

content.passageText:
XII. The Supreme Court’s ruling on the protection of the Great Indian Bustard (GIB), one of
the world’s most endangered bird species, has emerged as a significant moment in India’s
evolving climate and environmental jurisprudence. The case arose from concerns that overhead
power transmission lines in arid regions of Rajasthan and Gujarat posed a fatal risk to the GIB,
which has poor frontal vision and is prone to collision. The Court initially directed that all
power lines in identified habitats be placed underground, prioritising species survival over
infrastructural convenience. However, the judgment also exposed the complex intersection
between biodiversity protection and climate action. Renewable energy projects, particularly
solar and wind installations, often rely on extensive transmission infrastructure. Critics argued
that an inflexible undergrounding mandate could severely delay India’s clean energy targets,
increase costs, and undermine climate mitigation efforts. Responding to these concerns, the
Court modified its earlier approach. It acknowledged that environmental governance cannot
operate through rigid binaries of conservation versus development. Instead, it emphasised a
principle of “informed balancing,” requiring authorities to consider ecological sensitivity,
technological feasibility, cost, and climate commitments together. The Court directed the
creation of an expert committee to assess where undergrounding is necessary and where
alternative mitigation measures, such as bird diverters- may suffice. This reflects a broader
judicial shift from absolute prohibitions to adaptive, evidence-based regulation. Importantly,
the Court recognised that climate change itself threatens biodiversity, implying that poorly
designed conservation orders may paradoxically worsen long-term environmental outcomes if
they obstruct renewable energy deployment. The ruling, therefore, reframes environmental
protection as a constitutional obligation that must be harmonised with climate goals. It signals
that courts will scrutinise executive action (or inaction) in climate matters, but will also exercise
restraint by deferring to scientific expertise where appropriate. Rather than prescribing uniform
solutions, the judgment promotes context-specific governance, reinforcing the idea that
sustainable development requires continuous calibration between competing environmental
imperatives, not categorical trade-offs.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.ceew.in/blogs/what-does-supreme-
court-ruling-on-protecting-great-indian-bustard-species-mean-for-climate-change-legislation,
23-05-2024

options:
The Court concluded that biodiversity protection must always yield to economic
      growth.

The Court recognised that rigid conservation measures could undermine climate
      mitigation goals.

The Court accepted that renewable energy projects are immune from environmental
      scrutiny.
Both A and C.

the world’s most endangered bird species, has emerged as a significant moment in India’s
evolving climate and environmental jurisprudence. The case arose from concerns that overhead
power transmission lines in arid regions of Rajasthan and Gujarat posed a fatal risk to the GIB,
which has poor frontal vision and is prone to collision. The Court initially directed that all
power lines in identified habitats be placed underground, prioritising species survival over
infrastructural convenience. However, the judgment also exposed the complex intersection
between biodiversity protection and climate action. Renewable energy projects, particularly
solar and wind installations, often rely on extensive transmission infrastructure. Critics argued
that an inflexible undergrounding mandate could severely delay India’s clean energy targets,
increase costs, and undermine climate mitigation efforts. Responding to these concerns, the
Court modified its earlier approach. It acknowledged that environmental governance cannot
operate through rigid binaries of conservation versus development. Instead, it emphasised a
principle of “informed balancing,” requiring authorities to consider ecological sensitivity,
technological feasibility, cost, and climate commitments together. The Court directed the
creation of an expert committee to assess where undergrounding is necessary and where
alternative mitigation measures, such as bird diverters- may suffice. This reflects a broader
judicial shift from absolute prohibitions to adaptive, evidence-based regulation. Importantly,
the Court recognised that climate change itself threatens biodiversity, implying that poorly
designed conservation orders may paradoxically worsen long-term environmental outcomes if
they obstruct renewable energy deployment. The ruling, therefore, reframes environmental
protection as a constitutional obligation that must be harmonised with climate goals. It signals
that courts will scrutinise executive action (or inaction) in climate matters, but will also exercise
restraint by deferring to scientific expertise where appropriate. Rather than prescribing uniform
solutions, the judgment promotes context-specific governance, reinforcing the idea that
sustainable development requires continuous calibration between competing environmental
imperatives, not categorical trade-offs.

court-ruling-on-protecting-great-indian-bustard-species-mean-for-climate-change-legislation,

content.passageText:
XIII. In contract law, the distinction between void and voidable contracts is fundamental to
understanding when legal obligations arise and when they can be avoided. A void contract is
one that is invalid from its very inception. It creates no legal rights or obligations because it
lacks one or more essential elements of a valid contract, such as a lawful object, lawful
consideration, or capacity of the parties. Agreements that are illegal, opposed to public policy,
or impossible to perform are classic examples. Since a void contract is a legal nullity, it cannot
be enforced by either party, and ratification is not possible. A voidable contract, on the other
hand, is a valid and enforceable contract unless and until it is avoided by the party entitled to
do so. Such contracts usually suffer from defects in free consent. When consent is caused by
coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake as to fact, the law allows the
aggrieved party to either affirm the contract or rescind it. Until this choice is exercised, the
contract remains legally binding. The distinction has important practical consequences. In void
agreements, restitution is generally unavailable because the law does not recognise the
transaction. In contrast, when a voidable contract is rescinded, the parties may be required to
restore benefits received. Another key difference lies in enforceability by third parties: rights
cannot flow from a void agreement, whereas third-party rights may arise under a voidable
contract before it is rescinded. Thus, while void contracts reflect situations where the law
refuses recognition altogether, voidable contracts represent situations where the law protects
consent but leaves the final choice to the injured party. Understanding this difference ensures
clarity in determining remedies, enforceability, and the stability of contractual relationships.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://cleartax.in/s/difference-between-void-and-
voidable-contract, 21-04-2025

content.passageText:
XIV. The growing debate on whether children should be allowed unrestricted access to social
media has brought child rights, parental autonomy, and state regulation into direct legal tension.
Several jurisdictions across the world have proposed or enacted minimum age requirements for
social media use, often coupled with parental consent mechanisms. The rationale behind such
regulation is grounded in mounting evidence linking excessive social media exposure to mental
health harms among children, including anxiety, cyberbullying, and addiction-like behaviour.
In India, the legal framework does not currently impose a blanket statutory age ban on social
media platforms. Instead, regulation emerges indirectly through data protection norms,
intermediary obligations, and child protection principles. The Digital Personal Data Protection
regime emphasises that children require heightened safeguards, recognising their limited
capacity to give informed consent. However, critics caution that imposing rigid age thresholds
risks paternalism and may infringe children’s evolving autonomy and freedom of expression.
A complete prohibition may also be ineffective, as children often bypass age gates through
misrepresentation. Courts examining such regulatory proposals are likely to apply a
proportionality analysis. The State must demonstrate that age-based restrictions pursue a
legitimate aim, are rationally connected to child welfare, are the least restrictive means
available, and balance benefits against harms to fundamental freedoms. Alternatives such as
parental control tools, algorithmic safeguards, and platform accountability are increasingly
viewed as less restrictive measures. The constitutional challenge lies in recognising children as
rights-bearing individuals while acknowledging their vulnerability. The legal question is not
whether children should be protected from harm, but how such protection can be achieved
without unjustifiably curtailing autonomy, expression, and access to information in the digital
age.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.livelaw.in/articles/social-media-age-
limit-for-children-analysis-514007, 20-12-2025

XV. Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution
occupies a central position in democratic life. In a recent observation, the Supreme Court
reminded both citizens and governments that the value of free speech lies not merely in its
availability but in society’s willingness to tolerate dissent, disagreement, and even discomfort.
The Court emphasised that constitutional freedoms are not meant only for agreeable or popular
opinions; they protect unpopular, critical, and minority viewpoints as well. Suppressing speech
merely because it causes offence or embarrassment to those in power risks hollowing out the


democratic promise of the Constitution. At the same time, the Court clarified that freedom of
speech is not absolute. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of
sovereignty, public order, decency, morality, and other specified grounds. However, the Court
warned that these restrictions cannot become routine tools of convenience. Governments must
demonstrate a clear nexus between the speech sought to be restricted and the harm
apprehended. Vague allegations, speculative threats, or broad claims of disturbance cannot
justify curtailment. The responsibility to respect free speech, the Court noted, rests as much on
the State as on citizens, who must learn to engage with opposing views without immediately
demanding censorship. The judgment also underlined an institutional concern: frequent resort
to criminal law against speech risks creating a chilling effect, where individuals self-censor out
of fear rather than legal prohibition. Such an environment undermines constitutional culture.
Ultimately, the Court’s intervention frames free speech as a shared constitutional commitment.
While the State may regulate expression in exceptional circumstances, the default
constitutional posture must remain one of restraint, tolerance, and faith in democratic dialogue
rather than suppression.

XVI. Climate change is no longer treated in international law as a peripheral environmental
concern; it is increasingly understood as a structural force reshaping the architecture of the
international legal order itself. Traditionally, international law was organised around discrete
subject-matter silos, environmental law, human rights law, trade law, law of the sea, each
governed by its own treaties, institutions, and principles. Climate change disrupts this
compartmentalisation because its causes, impacts, and remedies cut across all these domains
simultaneously. This has produced a gradual but profound transformation in how international
legal obligations are framed. Climate-related duties are no longer confined to specific
environmental treaties but increasingly inform the interpretation of existing norms in human
rights, state responsibility, and international economic law. For example, obligations
concerning the right to life, health, and housing are now interpreted in light of climate
vulnerability, particularly for small island states and future generations. Similarly, principles
of due diligence and prevention, once applied narrowly to transboundary pollution, are being
expanded to address cumulative and long-term climate harms. Another structural shift lies in
the changing role of courts and quasi-judicial bodies. International and domestic courts are
increasingly asked to adjudicate climate-related claims, not merely as policy questions but as
legal disputes involving enforceable obligations. This judicial engagement challenges the
traditional view that climate action lies solely within political discretion. At the same time,
climate litigation tests the limits of causation, attribution, and jurisdiction, forcing courts to


adapt existing legal doctrines to complex scientific realities. Importantly, climate change also
alters the balance between sovereignty and cooperation. While states remain formally
sovereign, effective climate governance requires collective action, shared responsibility, and
differentiated obligations based on capacity and historical emissions. This tension reveals a
shift from a purely consent-based system toward a more relational understanding of
international law, where global risks generate expectations of conduct even in the absence of
explicit consent. Thus, climate change functions as a catalyst for a structural reorientation of
international law pushing it from fragmented rule-making toward integrated, systemic
reasoning that foregrounds interdependence, responsibility, and long-term planetary interests.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://voelkerrechtsblog.org/climate-change-at-the-
forefront-of-the-structural-transformation-of-international-law/, 04-08-2025

LOGICAL REASONING
XV.India has billions online - yet homegrown messaging apps remain rare. Arattai is catching
eyes, but can it move beyond the buzz to challenge WhatsApp or will it fizzle out like Koo?
Indian social media apps often stumble because they fall short on the essentials: tech, business
and innovation. The tech architecture of a successful social media app is not difficult to
replicate. The business model is also established around targeted advertising, which is again
not a barrier. The summit lies in the creative expression of users, where most Indian apps
struggle with originality. Copycat versions of established media platforms can't break their
network power despite having a large potential customer base. The lack of innovation has posed
the biggest challenge to the development of homegrown social media, although technical
support and monetisation strategies have also contributed to the overall gloom.

The holy grail for media platforms is creating a new form of content that activates the network
effect. As content tech evolves, it opens a wide field of innovative social communication. The
ability to pull all existing and emerging content formats onto one platform, however, does not
ensure success. Community development requires special effort through discoverability, where
the tech backend comes into play.

The safe course in building an SM platform is to offer a bundle of services that includes content
sharing. Instead of betting on the next TikTok, tech companies are more comfortable
developing a WeChat-like platform that offers a broad range of services, from shopping to
playing games. In either case, Chinese app developers have shown the way to break Silicon
Valley's stranglehold over social media. Indian apps, unfortunately, score poorly on both
convenience and creativity, which makes every new attempt at a social media breakthrough a
heartbreaking effort. Then again, all it takes is one success. Social media will remain a dynamic
medium, keeping hopes alive for the eventual arrival of an Indian champion.

LOGICAL REASONING
XV.India has billions online - yet homegrown messaging apps remain rare. Arattai is catching
eyes, but can it move beyond the buzz to challenge WhatsApp or will it fizzle out like Koo?
Indian social media apps often stumble because they fall short on the essentials: tech, business
and innovation. The tech architecture of a successful social media app is not difficult to
replicate. The business model is also established around targeted advertising, which is again
not a barrier. The summit lies in the creative expression of users, where most Indian apps
struggle with originality. Copycat versions of established media platforms can't break their
network power despite having a large potential customer base. The lack of innovation has posed
the biggest challenge to the development of homegrown social media, although technical
support and monetisation strategies have also contributed to the overall gloom.

The holy grail for media platforms is creating a new form of content that activates the network
effect. As content tech evolves, it opens a wide field of innovative social communication. The
ability to pull all existing and emerging content formats onto one platform, however, does not
ensure success. Community development requires special effort through discoverability, where
the tech backend comes into play.

The safe course in building an SM platform is to offer a bundle of services that includes content
sharing. Instead of betting on the next TikTok, tech companies are more comfortable
developing a WeChat-like platform that offers a broad range of services, from shopping to
playing games. In either case, Chinese app developers have shown the way to break Silicon
Valley's stranglehold over social media. Indian apps, unfortunately, score poorly on both
convenience and creativity, which makes every new attempt at a social media breakthrough a
heartbreaking effort. Then again, all it takes is one success. Social media will remain a dynamic
medium, keeping hopes alive for the eventual arrival of an Indian champion.

content.passageText:
XVI. Over 20 years ago, when Maria Corina Machado first confronted Venezuela’s deep
institutional rot, she knew the choice was clear: It would be ballots over bullets. As she
challenged the authoritarian regimes of Hugo Chavez and his successor Nicolas Maduro,
demanding free and fair elections and campaigning against their repressive measures, she was
tried for treason, stripped of her seat in the National Assembly, repeatedly threatened with
physical violence, barred from election and forced to go into hiding. That she has never
stopped speaking up and reaching out to her beleaguered fellow citizens is a measure of her
great personal courage. For the Nobel Committee, which has honoured her long fight with the
Peace Prize for 2025, it is also an exemplar of what it takes to keep the flame of democracy
alive.

At a time of deepening authoritarianism around the world, this year’s Peace Prize
acknowledges that the work of democracy is never done, that it must be defended as much
against tyranny as against cynicism and indifference. Democracy, as the Nobel Committee
has said, “depends on people who refuse to stay silent, who dare to step forward despite grave
risk and who remind us that freedom must never be taken for granted”. The refusal to be mute
in the face of despotism and cruelty often comes at great personal cost — imprisonment,
exile, violence and even death — but this is what makes the fight so precious. Peace, of
course, is not just the absence of war. Peace can exist only where there is freedom, where
people have the right to choose and where they have a voice and hand in shaping their
nation’s future. The honouring of Machado’s tireless efforts to restore democracy in her
country is an endorsement of the fact that the work of peace is not just conducted at the high
diplomatic table; it happens in the trenches of the everyday struggle for justice and in the
labour of all those who resist tyranny at every level.

machado-shows-democracy-is-a-work-in-progress-10300026/
